items.body: Omar Sosa - 'Sendas' / a RootsWorld review Omar Sosa Sendas Otá digital Interview and review by Michael Stone Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa’s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa’s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , “Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras… like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.” “Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don’t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.” “I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.” Sosa laughs, “My son says, ‘Your niche is really small.’ But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.” “Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category — and so do many music journalists! The industry’s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.” “But I play to be free of that,” Sosa says. “I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That’s the take, the natural voice of your soul. ‘Less is more’ is a mantra in my life and music.” Consider the opening of “Inside the Spirit,” easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance — only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, “Deities Serenade” is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener’s own self-location. “Inside My Soul” and “Something from Home” are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin’s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa “Caribbean Movement” and “Shirma” speak to Sosa’s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world’s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa’s music to words is rather a fool’s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa’s longtime manager and friend relates, “We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.” Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues. Find the artist online.
items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa的专辑《Sendas》展现了高度个人化的实验性即兴创作。作品在意大利Fazioli钢琴音乐厅录制，全程两小时即兴演奏完成，后期融入人声采样、打击乐、循环音效和实地录音等元素。音乐融合了爵士、拉美、古典及世界音乐语汇，同时借鉴了喉音唱法等人声技巧。Sosa在创作中刻意规避风格标签，追求无拘无束的表达方式，强调首take的自然灵魂感。这张专辑与用户的实验/前卫和学院派爵士口味高度契合，跨领域融合特征明显，创新的声音设计和即兴手法增添了独特的艺术价值。

items.excerpt: Dave Douglas has spent a career dodging his own shadow, and that restlessness is precisely what keeps his catalog from ever feeling stagnant. Transcend locates its friction point between two titans who seem unlikely to share the same oxygen: the spiritual grandeur of Duke Ellington's Sacred Concerts and the dense, mosaic canvases of painter Jack Whitten.
items.body:
Dave Douglas has spent a career dodging his own shadow, and that restlessness is precisely what keeps his catalog from ever feeling stagnant. Transcend locates its friction point between two titans who seem unlikely to share the same oxygen: the spiritual grandeur of Duke Ellington's Sacred Concerts and the dense, mosaic canvases of painter Jack Whitten.

The weight of the album rests on the chemistry of this specific quintet. With James Brandon Lewis on tenor, Tomeka Reid on cello, Rafiq Bhatia on guitar, and Ian Chang on drums, the music moves away from a traditional leader-and-sidemen setup toward something genuinely collective. Reid is a fresh voice in Douglas's orbit, and she fundamentally shifts the group's architecture. Cello can often feel like a novelty in jazz, but Reid integrates it so seamlessly into the harmonic floor that you quickly forget the instrument and simply hear the depth it adds.

The set opens with Ellington's "Come Sunday," played with a grit that favors atmosphere over reverence. Douglas avoids the trap of making the melody too precious. Instead, Bhatia's distortion-laced guitar rolls in like a storm front while Lewis enters with that signature, forceful tenor sound, pushing just enough against the melody to keep it from settling. The originals carry even more weight, particularly "Energy Fields," which feels unsettled in the best way as Chang drives a nervous pulse from underneath while Reid and Bhatia tangle in tactile textures, the whole thing morphing into Douglas' intense proclamations.

On "Gentle Collapse," Whitten's influence is most tangible—melodic fragments appear, dissolve, and reassemble in altered forms, mimicking the layered surfaces and broken symmetry of Whitten's canvases. "Heaven" serves as the emotional hinge, featuring Douglas and Lewis circling one another in near unisons that never quite lock. That microscopic gap between their notes is where the real drama lives, generating a sustained tension that only partially resolves.

Not everything lands with equal force. "Argle-Bargle" aims for a specific kind of jagged friction, but the moving parts never quite click into place. It feels more like eavesdropping on an interesting process than arriving at a satisfying payoff. Ellington's "Oclupaca," however, provides a welcome rhythmic snap to a set that often prefers texture over momentum.

Douglas skips the big theatrical finish and simply lets the sound evaporate into the room—a move that feels less like a conclusion and more like a mark of genuine confidence, trusting the listener to find their own way out.
items._cn_summary: 当代爵士与实验音乐的跨界融合之作，以Duke Ellington的精神性圣乐传统和抽象表现主义画家Jack Whitten的视觉语言为双重参照，构建出层次丰富的声响景观。由James Brandon Lewis、Tomeka Reid、Rafiq Bhatia、Ian Chang组成的五重奏摒弃传统领奏结构，实现真正的集体即兴。大提琴的融入打破了爵士乐队的常规声部配置，电子音效的运用增添了现代感。专辑在氛围营造、结构解构与即兴张力之间寻求平衡，整体艺术视野开阔。部分曲目如「Energy Fields」和「Gentle Collapse」展现了高度的实验性与原创性，而「Argle-Bargle」等曲目的实验意图虽明确但执行略显不足。作为资深音乐人Dave Douglas的最新探索，这张专辑在传统爵士框架内注入了前沿意识，适合关注学院派爵士与实验融合的听众。

items.body:
As if producer and archival sleuth Zev Feldman weren't already busy enough unearthing lost jazz treasures, he has recently launched a new imprint, Time Traveler. A devoted collector in his own right, Feldman has turned his attention—at least initially—to the storied catalog of Muse Records. Founded in 1972 by Joe Fields, with significant contributions from Don Schlitten, Muse weathered the shifting tides of the industry for a quarter century. While portions of the catalog have resurfaced on CD over the years, Time Traveler now delivers these titles back to their intended analog format, marking their first vinyl reissues since the original pressings.

Following earlier Muse revivals featuring Roy Brooks, Carlos Garnett, Kenny Barron, Larry Young/Joe Chambers, and Woody Shaw, Buster Williams' Pinnacle receives the Record Store Day treatment. This 1975 session is presented with care: mastering by Matt Lutthans, pressing at Optimal Media, a Stoughton tip-on jacket, and newly commissioned liner notes accompanied by a period photograph of Williams.

Recorded in the wake of Williams' tenure with Herbie Hancock's groundbreaking Mwandishi ensemble, Pinnacle carries forward many of that group's exploratory, groove-oriented sensibilities. The expansive opener, "The Hump," unfolds with a serpentine pulse, its bass clarinet textures and collective improvisation later finding new life through sampling by The Fugees and A Tribe Called Quest. Williams' bass navigates the shifting Latin undercurrents of "Noble Ego," enriched by wordless vocals and the percussive colors of Guilherme Franco. The title track closes side one with a striking, angular theme voiced by trumpet, saxophones, and ensemble vocals, with both Shaw and Sonny Fortune contributing concise but memorable solos.

Side two opens with the fluid, gliding lines of "Tayamisha," where Williams' melodic sensibility gives way to a firmly swinging feel. Fortune's soprano cuts through with angular phrasing, while Onaje Allan Gumbs adds depth on acoustic piano, supported throughout by the responsive drumming of Billy Hart. Any notion that straight-ahead swing had fallen out of favor in the 1970s is quickly dispelled. The shimmering Rhodes textures of "Batuki" bring the session to a close, its laid-back funk underscored by Fortune's luminous flute work and an especially commanding presence from Shaw's trumpet.

Ultimately, Pinnacle stands as a vivid reminder of a fertile, often underappreciated period in jazz. With this thoughtfully produced reissue, Feldman once again makes a compelling case for revisiting the margins of the canon—where, more often than not, the real discoveries await.
items._cn_summary: 1975年爵士录音，Buster Williams在Herbie Hancock Mwandishi乐队之后的探索之作。专辑延续了70年代实验爵士的即兴传统与groove导向，融合拉丁节奏、集体即兴与非线性结构。低音单簧管、Rhodes电钢琴、非洲-拉丁打击乐等元素构建出层次丰富的声响空间，部分曲目被嘻哈艺人采样引用。Side One以探索性见长，Side Two回归更直接的摇摆风格，整体呈现70年代爵士特有的实验精神与商业可听性的平衡。Time Traveler厂牌的独立再版制作精良，忠实还原了原始录音的质感。对于关注实验爵士与自由即兴的听众而言，这张被低估的遗产值得深入发掘。

items.body: Review by Finnforest — A Most Welcome Reprieve Stumbling half-conscious through the wreckage of mid-80s Banco, one could be forgiven for despairwhile pondering what could possibly follow E Via, the 1985 album that many figured must bethe end of the progressive juggernaut, for real this time. After all, it made 90125 andGenesis Shapes seem like masterpiece-level material by comparison. E Via had hit melike the worst moments of Chicago 17 and Invisible Touch put through a blender. I felt ready to liedown and embrace the end when, out of absolute nowhere, arrives Donna Plautilla. I don't know who Donna is supposed to be historically, but to me she was an angel of mercy in thismoment of Banco's discog. While dropping in 1989, the archival material was actually recorded 20years earlier by the newly-formed Banco of the late '60s: the Nocenzi brothers, the Falco brothers,and Franco Pontecorvi. This is embryonic Banco music and, despite falling well short of the grandeurof their acclaimed 72-73 albums, it is nonetheless absolutely enjoyable proto-prog in the same veinas the first Yes album, From Genesis to Revelation, Ad Gloriam, and '60s Deep Purple.Yes, it is dated now and has a little bit of that '60s Iron Butterfly psych vibe and short songsformat that place it well short of something like Darwin, but even without Francesco DiGiacomo's vocal talent, one can still hear the beginnings of what might follow. The album is wellrecorded and mixed, so it sounds pretty fab considering the age and, at that point, unknown statureof the group. The tracks here are keyboard-led period rock that is slightly less adventurous than, say, the Yesdebut, but only slightly, and it quite nicely preludes the RPI movement that was soon coming.Without Di Giacomo in the fold at this point, the vocals are handled by Vittorio Nocenzi, and whilehe lacks the legendary Di Giacomo's pipes, the fact is that he does just fine. He's no slouch as asinger, and he has backing from the Falco brothers (who were from the band Crash). As you mightimagine, the songs have that certain Italian spice that informs the music, from the beautifullanguage to the all-too-brief classical guitar and flute and harpsichord moments. Otherwise thesongs are driven by great piano and organ runs backed by upbeat, grooving rhythm section. I love thebold and up-front bass by Fabrizio Falco. The songs may indeed be proto-prog, but they are neverboring or lacking enthusiasm. The tunes are engaging and well composed and not as dated in the "flowery sense" as otherpeer '60s "organ rock." Is this album going to change your world? Likely not, but it is a really nice gem for the Banco fangenerally, the chance to hear them in this developing stage and with good audio quality. Perhaps mypraise of this album is partially the result of being bludgeoned into near catatonic haze by EVia, with Donna by contrast coming across as some kind of manna from heaven due to myE Via waterboarding. I can't say. But I had a good time with Donna, whoever she was. Ihighly recommend this early glimpse of RPI for the sheer joy of the playing and obvious burgeoningcreativity. It's slam dunk 3 stars, and I'm right on the edge of going 4.
items._cn_summary: 意大利前卫摇滚乐团Banco del Mutuo Soccorso的早期录音合辑，录制于1960年代末至1970年代初，1989年正式发行。作品展现了该乐团尚未完全成熟时期的音乐形态，属于proto-prog（原生前卫摇滚）风格，融合了早期Yes、Genesis及60年代Deep Purple的影响，同时加入了意大利特有的古典吉他、长笛和羽管键琴等元素。键盘主导的编曲配合富有节奏感的贝斯线条，呈现出带有意大利风情的时期摇滚特征。作为前卫摇滚的重要产地作品，该专辑对于了解意大利前卫摇滚发展脉络具有一定参考价值，但相较于乐团72-73年的成熟期作品，实验性和复杂度较为有限，更接近于带有古典元素的前卫流行曲式。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — This version of Yes, with Jon Anderson singing so differently, so jazzy and psychedelic, already featuring Chris Squire, Bill Bruford, and Peter Banks with that variety of sounds... they would have stood out in the sea of ​​bands of the '60s even if they hadn't been the Yes we later knew. They weren't Beatles clones like so many others... and it was a different band, of course! Just listen to the acoustic ending of "Beyond and Before." And "I See You" is one of my favorite tracks... vocal harmonies in a jazzy, psychedelic context, Jon with a voice that sometimes sounded like many jazz singers at once, even Billie Holiday! Sometimes it's just the guitar and drums... and I think they were already a mature band of experienced musicians; in fact, several of them came from previous bands, and they only pale in comparison to their own future work... which was so different from what they were doing, despite the classical influences already present in Banks' solos.So what standard, what parameter to use? That of the progressive context? If so, the result would be uneven because some works were already pointing in that direction without even knowing it, while others, equally beautiful like Yesterday and Today, were more anchored in the 60s. Although that is precisely where the magic of this debut lies, its freshness, its variety...its honesty.Looking Around shows a mixed maturity, achieved in the instrumental aspect, in the execution, but not yet in the compositional aspect, where one could expect more originality in the arrangements, although the embryo of a more mature band is already present in The Yes Album years later.Harold Land displays an attempt at more complex, distinctly British composition, which, however, is light years away from the classic Yes style. Banks' guitar arrangements are impeccable, and Jon's voice is perfectly on point, emotive and epic... yet understated at the same time, which is what a song of this magnitude demands. "Every Little Thing" begins the final trio of tracks, which are also my favorites. When they stray from the script and Banks plays without following it, and Bruford follows him blindly, it's a different band, rawer, another good band with people we know, with nods to the Beatles that remain just that. And yet, the final result is uneven due to small details, such as unpredictable parts alongside others that are quite foreseeable and detract from the impact of the latter. In Sweetness you can enjoy Jon's clean and tender voice, Chris's bass, Paul Banks' guitar and Bill who could play with brushes or the edges like Brazilian bossa nova drummers, but it was still a little way off, you enjoy that previous experiment, which was definitely still a promise of what was to come...seemingly impossible to isolate oneself from the context...something that could be done with I see you.It goes without saying that Bill Bruford loves jazz... and Jon, throughout his career, has systematically returned to it like an old friend he may not see often, but whose affection remains undiminished. He has always demonstrated his attachment to the genre, whether on his second solo album, Song of Seven, or with the studio tracks on Keys to Ascension, or his collaboration with Jean-Luc Ponty a few years ago. This debut also speaks to that, and therein lies its value, beyond its level within the progressive standard.Survival has that unique magic of Swinging London...from that photo shoot with those statues in the album booklet...that makes it eternal, that never ages.
items._cn_summary: 1969年交响前卫摇滚乐队Yes的首张专辑，融合了爵士、迷幻与古典元素。评论指出Jon Anderson的声线具有爵士歌手特质，Bill Bruford展现了爵士影响，Peter Banks的吉他编排兼具古典与迷幻色彩。专辑虽处于乐队风格的探索期，存在编排不均衡、部分段落过于可预测等问题，但已展现出跨类型融合的潜力。作为1969年的作品，其实验性与诚实态度使其在同期作品中脱颖而出，尽管距后来经典阵容的成熟风格仍有差距。

items.body: RL Huber of Eureka Springs, Arkansas has an orchestral sound, with abundant strings and pianos, and a classical-drone crossover feeling that is complex and subtle. Meditation drones elevated in some sunny mountains Sea Legs by RL Huber   RL Huber of Eureka Springs, Arkansas has an orchestral sound, with abundant strings and pianos, and a classical-drone crossover feeling that is complex and subtle. The title “Sea Legs” makes me think of learning to walk through the relentless bobbing motion on a boat in rough waters; contrast this with the sound here, which makes me think of meditation drones elevated in some sunny mountains, a classical ambient avant-garde terrestrial sojourn. It is all very curious and lovely, in a very peculiar way. The longer ambient composition has a sustained tone style, a slow series of long notes using what sounds like traditional classical string instruments. The entire orchestra focuses on one note that changes every few moments, slowly taking form, “Sea Legs” (9:17). Long silky drones that shift, now a piano emerges with the same concept, one note holds then another note comes along, the way that the notes change, the intervals are similar, creating the feeling of slow twilight music. “Slowly Traversing the Wall” (5:14) is a drone / field recording piece, I hear a slow gravelly hiss, a distant foghorn, wind. There could be a brief sustained piano note in the mix, perhaps a slow drone nocturne. The closing track, “Silt and Sand” (3:49) begins with a bit of distortion and wistfulness, nestled with beloved bowed tones. The song title suggests that we are on the beach, feeling the textures of the grains. “I have been recording experimental music since 2004 using project names such as Vopat, Olekranon and Sujo as well as my own name, Ryan Huber. I have recorded a number of albums in the electronic, noise and drone genres. Memories of Falling incorporates these elements with a more restrained approach. I have been influenced by modern artists such as John Cage, Tim Hecker and Anna Thorvaldsdottir.”There are nine RL Huber releases available on Bandcamp, including Sea Legs, Themisto, Glass House Architecture, Dagos, Hafgufa, Forgiving Light, Return of the Cosmonaut, Memories of Falling, and Animan Edere.Eureka Springs is a city in the Ozark Mountains of northwest Arkansas, known for the preserved Victorian buildings of its Historic District, such as the Palace Bath House, Basin Park Hotel and Crescent Hotel, all built around the city’s natural springs. In the nearby hills, soaring Thorncrown Chapel is a striking wood and glass church. To the south, Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge is home to big cats and bears. Sea Legs is available on Bandcamp. Sea Legs by RL Huber
items._cn_summary: RL Huber来自阿肯色州尤里卡泉，独立发行了这张融合古典弦乐与嗡鸣/氛围实验的专辑《Sea Legs》。音乐以持续的长音符、丝滑的嗡鸣为基底，辅以钢琴与弦乐的古典音色，营造出冥想式的聆听体验。九首曲目中，主打作品以缓慢渐变的音调构建出类似暮光的氛围，田野录音与嗡鸣的结合又增添了环境音景的质感。专辑在实验音乐框架下融入当代古典的美学追求，体现了创作者自2004年以来的实验音乐积淀。作品与小众独立发行厂牌的特质相符，对于偏好实验与当代古典交叉领域的听众而言具有较高的契合度。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Considered one of the pillars of the Rock Urbano scene in Spain, the Madrid based LE�O (means "log"of all things!) emerged from one of the progenitors of the style, �u in which founder and frontmanRosendo Mercado played guitar from 1974-77 before he butted heads with the notoriously difficultJose Carlos Molina and left before that band's debut "Cuentos De Ayer Y De Hoy" hit the market.While it would take a while to regroup, in 1978 the band was born and existed for five years untilthe Rock Urbano boom gave way to the increasing popularity of new wave and post-punk. Initiallyfeaturing Rosendo Mercado on guitar and vocals, Ramiro Penas on drums and Chiqui Mariscal on bass,Mariscal abruptly departed during the recording of the band's self-titled debut release and replacedby Tony Urbano. The power trio would remain intact for the rest of the band's existence. Due to someof the material being already recorded, both bassists appear on this debut release.The band's debut hit the scene in 1979 and featured a sound in the brackish waters where 70s progwas intertwined into a more contemporary hard rock / early heavy metal sound. One of thedistinguishing features of Rock Urbano was the use of the Spanish language in protest against theuniversal adoption of English as the lingua franca of the music industry. Spain was definitelyprotective of its indigenous features and this particular movement found a short burst of popularityaround the end of the 70s. LE�O's debut was a triumphant display of highly energetic melodic hardrock laced with raw guitar heft and crafty complex compositions that were reminiscent of similarlyminded acts from other nations such as Captain Beyond, Rush, Lucifer's Friend and Uriah Heep onlytaking things into even heavier territories threatening to launch the entire New Wave of BritishHeavy Metal Scene in the process.Consisting of seven tracks, this eponymous beginning featured extended prog-fueled instrumentalprowess in cahoots with vocal oriented hard rock heft and while the album in many ways exemplifies atypical heavier rock album of the late 70s. it is the unorthodox compositional approach that weavesunexpected tempo changes and labyrinthine journeys through certain longer tracks that keeps itplanted in the declining prog value system that had dominated the 70s but when this album wasreleased in 1979 finding a declining return value which is why the band would abandon these excesseson its sophomore album and jump on the more straightforward hard rock bandwagon. The album beginswith the sizzling guitar frenzy at the beginning of "Castigo" and remains fired up for most of its40 minute journey.While guitar riff churning is the usual modus operandi of LE�O's debut, slower more symphonic progmotifs do emerge such as on the atmospheric "La Nana" which is the most subdued track on board aswell as the acoustic guitar closer "Se Acab�!!!" which serves as a come down track from theadrenalized hard rock relentlessness that preceded. Considered a classic in the Spanish hard rockworld, LE�O unleashed an excellent slide of proggy hard rock on this cleverly crafted debut thatseems to pay tribute to the prog fueled 70s while recognizing the hard rock / heavy metal 80ssimultaneously. While the band's lyrics are exclusively in Spanish, the album is also notable forsocial criticism and other once taboo subject matter that were utterly banned before Franco's deathin 1975. It's definitely a hallmark of Spanish hard rock and sets itself apart from much of thegeneric competition. Very much in the vein of �u only without the Tull-ish flute and folk flavors.
items._cn_summary: 西班牙马德里乐队LEÃO的1979年同名专辑处于70年代前卫摇滚与硬摇滚/早期重金属的交汇地带。专辑融合了器乐化的渐进式编曲与强劲的吉他riff，被认为是西班牙Rock Urbano运动的代表作品之一，填补了当年前卫摇滚式微后的市场空白。专辑收录七首曲目，包含复杂的不规则节奏变化与叙事性强的长曲结构，同时保持了硬摇滚的动能感和旋律性。西班牙语演唱体现了本土文化自觉性，与用户偏好中世界音乐和实验前卫方向有一定交集，但在当代电子、爵士或暗潮元素上并无涉及。整体而言，这是一张具有地区文化价值的前卫硬摇滚专辑，编曲扎实但创新性相对保守，更接近传统70年代摇滚范式而非当代实验语境。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Clicked 5, but really 4.5...4 is just too low.Elder is a band founded in Boston in 2005, but has been based in Berlin, Germany for several years now. Their seventh full-length solo album, "Through Zero", is set to be released on May 29, 2026. I want to thank Jadd from Blues Funeral records (the band's US label) and Austin Griswold of Secret Service PR agency for providing me with a review copy. As always, I receive no further compensation, and this is a cold listen. I always call it like I hear it.Elder are known for their Heavy Psych Prog style. I have all of their albums since the 3rd album "Lore" from 2015 in my library and a smattering of tracks from their earlier work and have enjoyed a number of their songs. When I saw the buzz surrounding this release, however, I knew I had to reach out for a review copy. The album's six tracks range from 5:49-10:48.The lineup is:- Nicholas DiSalvo / guitar, vocals, synthesizer- Michael Risberg / guitar, Rhodes piano, slide guitar- Jack Donovan / bass guitar- Georg Edert / drums, percussion Time to jump in!Track 1 - Sigil to Ruin (10:39)The song begins with some quiet tones that fade in and slowly build until the band fully kicks in at about 25 seconds with a quick tempo heavy rhythmic groove. The guitars and synth play a melodic line over the steady pulse. At 1:45 an odd meter riff takes over as the music's dynamic level eases off. The full band returns to lead in the first vocals at around 2:20. The midrange vocals are draped with reverb and delays that fit the mood of the song nicely. I like how the track is in no hurry, taking its time to develop different themes and moods. Excellent heavy riffage kicks in at around 4:10. A bridge segment follows. A new section begins at around 6:20, heralded by delays that are panned hard to both speakers, giving a "ping-pong" effect; very cool! Just after 7 minutes a synth part takes over joined by drums with odd meter shifts. The electric piano begins to build around it, followed by tasty, delayed guitars then vocal harmonies. Just before 9 minutes, the music shifts again to a guitar solo over a new rhythm bed. This is very heavy, yet warm and spacious. After a big riff gives a final punctuation, the song winds down with various effects for the final several seconds. Outstanding opener!Track 2 - Capture/Releae (8:48)A warm synth chord fades in to commence the song. Sequenced synth patterns create a rhythm that is matched by the rhythm section. The rhythm is syncopated making it difficult to pin down the meter. At around 2:15, the music takes a turn for the heavy! After a short verse there is an instrumental section with meter-shifts-a-plenty. I love the harmonized guitar lines between vocal phrases in the next verse. At around 4 minutes, a "tribal" drumbeat provides the foundation for a bridge. At around 4:40, an instrumental break with guitar harmonies takes over. There are lots of juicy bits in this track for sure. Wow, the section that starts around 6:20 is really rockin'! Great guitar playing over the smokin' rhythm section. There is a lot going on here, in a very good way! The riffs are very fast and energetic, with nice smooth sustained guitar harmonies on the top as we approach the song's conclusion. Excellent cut!Track 3 - Through Zero (9:06)Let's see what the title track brings to the table. An arpeggiated guitar riff with a flanger, starts us off here. Then some very complex heavy riffing takes over with the rhythm section laying down an equally complex foundation. These guys really put the ROCK in Prog Rock. The first verse brings things down a good bit with minimal accompaniment initially, that builds up as we go along, with drums and bass entering. A heavy instrumental section follows. They are reminding me of a less angry Tool quite a bit here. I like the alternating light/heavy sections. At 4:00 a new 5-8 groove takes over. At around 5:15, layered guitars and distant vocal harmonies enter. I get the impression that the vocals are meant more as another layer of the soundscape at times. They become more prominent soon after. At around 6:35 there are some brain-tickling panned sounds for a few seconds before the band comes back hard and heavy. These guys are great at layering instrumental parts and stacking them up. While there are occasional standout guitar solos, the focus is more on tight, complex, ensemble playing. They seamlessly shift from one riff to the next before there is a final resolving chord then a repeating synth phrase. Another fantastic track!Track 4 - Strata (10:48)The synth from "Through Zero" leads us into this one. A low-pitched guitar riff joins it then the rhythm section joins in along with shimmering clean guitar parts on the top. The vocals come in at around 1:30 with minimal accompaniment. The harmonic structure of the vocals is somewhat akin to Alice in Chains. At around 3:35 a new, quick tempo guitar part takes over, to be joined by the rest of the band. Damn these guys are tight on the guitar harmonies while the rhythm section navigates all of the rhythmic twists and turns. These arrangements get quite dense at times, yet all of the parts can be discerned. I like the new riffs at around 7:30. The guitar solo on this one is a bit flashier than on the previous tracks. Then there is a major rhythm shift on a dime at 8:00 that made my head spin! It's a more straight-forward rock beat here. Things then smooth out a little at around 9 minutes. Just before the ten-minute mark they take it down to a low drone. Spacey synth lines close out the amazing song and take us into?Track 5 - Sight Unseen (8:50)The mellow synth parts continue gradually joined by guitar lines and a slowly building drum beat. They are really holding back here. Just before the three-minute point, however, the band comes in with some accents, but not in an overly heavy way. They then get into a Pink Floyd-like groove, if slightly heavier. So far, no vocals have appeared and we are past the halfway point. At just after 5:20 they start rockin' hard with odd meter riffs. What a great slow-burn instrumental this is turning out to be. With about one minute remaining, a sound effect shifts to a more mellow conclusion to our musical journey. Holy crap! What a ride that was!Track 6 - Blighted Age (5:49)The closing track brings acoustic guitar to the sound for the first time on the album, blended with a clean electric line. The vocals are smooth and I believe there are some conga drums initially providing the beat. The song begins to subtly build up in the second verse. At 2:15 things come back down. Electric piano enters shortly thereafter. There are some beautiful soundscapes being built here. This is a nice change of pace track to conclude the album on a more mellow note. Well-done.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is the third album I have reviewed in the past few days that is set to be released near the end of May; all three have been incredible! As noted earlier, this band isn't about being flashy and showcasing their individual talents, although there are some fleeting moments that tell me that they could do that if they chose to. Elder, as a band, show that they are committed to creating a collaborative sound, and they do it extremely well! This is making me want to go back and give some more attention to their earlier releases. Fans of Tool, heavier Rush and even heavier Porcupine Tree/Steven Wilson will likely really enjoy this album. I give it 4.5 out of 5 stars or 90%.
items._cn_summary: Elder是一支波士顿起源后移至柏林的重迷幻前卫摇滚乐队，专辑《Through Zero》延续其Heavy Psych Prog风格，融合奇数拍子、动态变化与合成器氛围。评论指出六首曲目均在5至10分钟区间，展现乐队对延展结构和渐进式构建的偏好。作品具备实验性元素与精密的编曲架构，融合延迟效果、合成器编排与重 riff，但整体风格相对传统，未在跨界融合上有突破性尝试。Blues Funeral Records为独立厂牌。适合对重迷幻和经典前卫摇滚有兴趣的听者。

items.body: Review by wbjazz — A stirring collection of late Emerson efforts, with noted soloists and orchestral contributions. In addition to numbers highlighted in Emerson's earlier "Three Fates Project" with Terje Mikkelsen, "Beyond the Stars" opens with moving performances by Rachel Flowers (on Toccata), Emerson's grandson Ethan (playing The Dreamer), and by Emerson himself, on the both the title track and "Glorietta Pass.""The Fugue" as a piano solo is given between parts one and two of "The Endless Enigma Suite." Following this (in the version posted to Bandcamp, at least) are the Alberto Ginastera-penned "Malambo," followed by guitarist Marc Bonilla's "The Mourning Sun", Emerson's "After All of This" and "Walking Distance", and Emerson's treatment of Copland's "Fanfare for the Common Man". A moving combination which may lead one to seek other numbers from the Emerson-Mikkelsen project, including their jazz-inflected "Tarkus Concertante", "Abaddon's Bolero", and Bonilla's "American Matador."Keith Emerson "Beyond the Stars"1. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是键盘大师基思·埃默森的晚期作品合集，属于跨界前卫摇滚风格。专辑收录了多首复杂编曲的曲目，包括《托卡塔》《无尽之谜组曲》等经典前卫摇滚作品，同时融入了copland的《普通人的号角》改编曲和吉纳斯特拉的《马拉博舞曲》。专辑由多位独奏家参与，突出了钢琴独奏与交响乐团的交织，既有前卫摇滚的技术性展示，也有古典音乐的结构性表达。对于偏好实验和前卫音乐的用户而言，这张专辑在融合交响元素和摇滚框架方面表现出一定的艺术性，但整体风格仍偏向传统跨界古典摇滚，未涉及电子或爵士即兴领域，融合的广度相对有限。

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Having overcome a certain disillusionment with the unexpected direction of "Mosquito" -less complex and more straightforward than the specialist critics and their fans had anticipated- Psychotic Waltz struck a balance two years later with "Bleeding" (1996), their fourth album. A mature work that recaptures some of the progressive complexity and darkness of the early "A Social Grace" and "Into the Everflow", whilst incorporating more defined structures and the gritty groove of the divisive "Mosquito".It is precisely the distinctive, pronounced bass of Phil Cuttino -replacing Ward Evans- that establishes, from the aggressive "Faded" onwards, together with the subtle shifts in dynamics and the syncopations of Norm Leggio's raw percussion, that elastic, driving rhythmic foundation which runs through much of the album: both for the dark atmospheres of the Sabbath-esque "Need" -featuring a great, ethereal guitar solo from the duo Brian McAlpin and Dan Rock- and for the ambient depths of the expansive "Sleep" -with another superb dual guitar performance- and the alternative "Skeleton", at times evoking the corrosive experimental textures of Tool; as well as the hypnotic scenes of the paranoid "Locust" and the mid-tempo melancholic "Bleeding", probably the two standout moments of the album.And the acoustic nuances are also present in the circus-like, rhythmic "Drift" and, above all, in the folk-tinged "My Grave" -a kindred spirit to Jethro Tull's medieval songbook and featuring what is arguably Buddy Lackey's finest vocal performance- breathing new life into an album that concludes with the instrumentally expansive, dense and emotionally restrained "Freedom?"."Bleeding" achieved great prestige within the underground scene, although -as was the case throughout Psychotic Waltz's entire discography- it failed to reach significant commercial success. That factor, coupled with ongoing financial difficulties and the growing divergence of the band members' musical and personal interests -with Buddy Lackey, now performing under the stage name Devon Graves, moving to Vienna to form Dead Soul Tribe- ultimately undermined the band's continuity, leading to its dissolution in early 1997. It would be 24 long years before the original members reunited and released "The God-Shaped Void" in 2020.4 stars
items._cn_summary: 《Bleeding》是Psychotic Waltz于1996年发行的第四张专辑，融合了前卫金属的复杂性、环境音乐的深度氛围以及民俗音乐的元素。专辑以Phil Cuttino标志性的贝斯线为核心，配合鼓手Norm Leggio的切分节奏构建出富有弹性的律动基础。音乐中既有Sabbach式黑暗重音和Tool式实验纹理，也有Jethro Tull风格的民谣段落，以及ambient氛围与双吉他的交织。Buddy Lackey的vocal表现出色，尤其在《My Grave》中将民谣与前卫融合。对于偏好实验前卫、黑暗氛围和跨领域融合的听众而言，这张专辑展现了90年代地下前卫金属的独特美学，虽未取得商业突破，但在地下圈子获得较高评价。

items.body: Review by Smurfreviews — Review #25Admittedly, I'm now familiar with many concept albums in the world of prog?and yet the second studio album by the Norwegian prog metal band "AVKRVST" has captivated me thematically. "Waving At The Sky," released back in 2025, deals with the joint abuse of children by two neighboring families. That sounds like absolutely heavy stuff, yet the band manages, through their chosen musical approach, to tackle this overwhelmingly oppressive theme with a masterful lightness without losing the heavy and dark focus. In doing so, the music exhibits various characteristics that I consider, during a 45-minute listening experience, to be a successful blend of different influences. The Norwegians' music clearly thrives on melodies. Whether these melodies are framed by symphonic lightness, rugged harshness, a warm retro sound, a modern art rock approach, or dissonant frenzy. What strikes me as particularly impressive with every listen is the skillful use of growls (though used very sparingly), which, for example, in the final long track provide a commendable contrast to the otherwise very harmonious and bombastic overall sound. Other highlights include the flute solo in the song "Conflating Memories" and Ross Jennings' guest vocals on "The Malevolent."Some reviews online criticize the band's lack of originality?but I cannot agree with this criticism and would like to encourage AKRVST to continue on their chosen musical path, because we all like to incorporate influences from other bands into our own music. And if this takes the form of Opeth, Riverside, Haken, and Porcupine Tree, then that's perfectly fine.Finally, the technical skill of the five band members must be highlighted?carefully combining a heavy theme with complex, light, and idiosyncratic passages requires a high level of musical competence, which the five musicians undoubtedly possess.An album absolutely worth listening to, not only for pure prog metal fans, but also for those who think outside the box...
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自挪威的渐进金属专辑，将沉重社会主题与复杂的编曲技巧相结合。音乐融合了重金属于交响、复古、艺术摇滚等多种元素，旋律线条突出，激烈的人声唱法与和谐宏大的整体音色形成对比。专辑呈现出渐进金属在北欧的发展面貌，兼具技术性与可听性，在保持实验性与主流接受度之间取得了平衡。整体制作出自独立厂牌，评论信息充足，能够体现乐队的音乐探索与风格融合特征。

items.body: “Division is the mission.” screensaver’s latest single, Division, is a synthpunk extravaganza wired for our collective calamity: a blast of motorik momentum that turns tribal panic, poisoned politics, and the ache for connection into something tense enough to dance to and ugly enough to believe. The Melbourne five-piece locks into a Krautrock push and lets the rest of the machinery misbehave: forceful synths, bass like a civic alarm, drums with no patience for your precious little feelings, and guitars that slash across the track with the clean nastiness of broken glass under fluorescent light. Krystal Maynard recites the lyrics like the latest dispatch from a culture choking on its own splintered team allegiances. The song’s refrain “Division is the mission” cuts deep, because it names division as design rather than accident: a strategy of fracture, distraction, and control hiding in plain sight. Around that line, screensaver builds a song about geopolitical fracture, attention rot, misinformation, environmental collapse, and the cheap tribal costume people wear when they have run out of better ideas. The band’s own explanation puts the song’s panic in plain terms: “Thematically, the lyrics hone in on the geopolitical state of the world. As the focus shifts perpetually and our attention is pulled in multiple directions, we’re left a fractured mess. We’re left divided by the distractions, crushed under the weight of a constant downpour of misinformation. The divide widens as we share the same space, the same air, the same earth. The very earth that we’re destroying in parallel as we fight against each other. Division is the mission and the powers that be are succeeding.” That is the horrorify gag, really. Everybody is trapped in the same room, while half of them are busy setting fire to the curtains and the other half are calling it discourse. The song’s sound has the clipped, bug-eyed intelligence of Devo, the political bite of The Clash, the sleek unease of Heaven 17, and the wired melodic twitch of XTC, though screensaver never sinks into costume-party pastiche. Christopher Stephenson, James Beck, Dorian Vary, Jonnine Nokes, and Maynard know how to make that synth-driven tension move. Julian Cue’s recording and mix keep every instrument close enough to bruise, while Casey Rice’s mastering gives the track a bright, hard finish, like metal warmed by catastrophe. The video, conceptualized by Maynard and directed and shot by James Beck, throws the song into a sick little cinema of social breakdown, examining “our allegiances, tribalism and the dichotomy of the individual vs the collective,” along with “the existential dread that haunts us all.” Its neo-noir dystopian grime and Romero-Fulci body-cluster chaos makes perfect sense beside the track’s thesis: groups form, groups splinter, and people drift between disconnection and disengagement while still yearning for contact. You might also spot a few familiar faces from the local Melbourne music scene among the pack. The zombies here are citizens, consumers, believers, skeptics, doomscrollers, neighbours. Nobody needs to eat flesh when they can chew through reality instead. “They’re not flesh eaters,” the band adds. “They are humans hungry for connection.” Watch the video for “Division” below: Released digitally through Poison City Records, Division is screensaver’s first new music since Three Lens Approach. It comes on like a public-service announcement from the end of the escalator. Tight, smart, agitated, and mean in all the right places, it positions screensaver as one of the sharper bands dragging post-punk discipline into synth-driven disorder. Listen to Division below and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 墨尔本后朋克乐队screensaver的单曲《Division》融合了Synthpunk与暗潮美学，呈现出带有政治批判性的声响景观。歌曲采用Krautrock式的机械推进节奏，结合尖锐的合成器线条与粗粝的吉他纹理，歌词聚焦于地缘政治分裂、信息洪流与部落主义等当代议题。制作层面保持独立厂牌的粗粝质感，人声念白式的表达强化了冷峻的警示氛围。音乐引用了Devo、The Clash、Heaven 17等新浪潮先驱的影响，但未陷入复古模仿，而是将复古元素融入当代语境。与用户偏好的暗潮、实验性路线存在一定契合度，政治性与合成器驱动的声音设计具有吸引力，整体作品在独立后朋克范畴内展现出高于平均的创新意识。

items.body: In the distance I am cold In the distance We’re growing old Casket Cassette’s Show Me a Sign is a song that illuminates the soul like a busted strip of Los Angeles nightlife, all neon nerves and cheap salvation. Constant Laval Williams has made a fine little art out of sounding stranded in public, which is harder than it sounds. Plenty of singers can do lonely. Fewer can do lonely while the beat is still carrying everybody’s boots across the dancefloor. This is the third new song from REDUCER, out June 12. Show Me a Sign is all reduction: emotion boiled until it stains the pan, desire shaved down to the bare request, survival turned into something blunt enough to fit in one hand. There is no grand cathedral of misery here, no velvet cape dragged theatrically through dry ice. The song wants a signal, a room, a body, a way back from whatever distance has turned the song’s protagonist cold and old before his time. Show Me a Sign channels the Medusa, Twist of Shadows, and Creatures era Clan of Xymox in its dusky romantic architecture, Cold Cave in its sleek black propulsion, and the frozen passion of The Danse Society and Pink Turns Blue, but Casket Cassette is smart enough to understand that influences should behave like a ghost at the bar, present but never picking up the tab. And the track moves with the clean, severe confidence of a dark priest descending inward into an icy sanctum, torchlit and severe, conjuring unspeakable visions as Williams’ voice cuts through the darkness. Lyrically, the song circles distance, exhaustion, and the stubborn will to continue after comfort has abandoned the room. The plea for a sign feels less like romantic longing than a last candle held against the cold, a small act of devotion made under pressure. Casket Cassette turns that ache into body music for the damaged and devout, for people who have been through Hell and back again and lived to tell the tale. Mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios and mastered by Stefan Brown at Abbey Road Studios, Show Me a Sign has a polished chill; every element has been placed with surgical precision: the beat advances, the synths flare and recede, and the vocal keeps its eyes open. The song’s desperation lands because it is sharpened rather than softened, with the production giving the plea force, shape, and urgency. Listen to Show Me a Sign below and order the single here. Show Me a Sign by Casket Cassette Casket Cassette will take The Reducer Tour across North America in summer 2026, with support from Stare Away and special guests. The run opens in Southern California before cutting through the Southwest and Texas, heading up the East Coast, crossing into Toronto, then moving through the Midwest, Mountain West, Pacific Northwest, and back down the West Coast, with a final date in California in November. items._cn_summary: 《Show Me a Sign》是Casket Cassette乐队的暗潮风格单曲，收录于2024年6月发行的专辑《REDUCER》。作品呈现典型的coldwave美学，以冷冽的合成器、简洁的鼓点与疏离的声线构建氛围。歌词聚焦距离感、疲惫与坚持的意志，将渴望联系的情绪转化为近乎仪式感的暗潮韵律。制作层面由Infinite Power Studios混音、Abbey Road Studios母带，确保了声音的精准定位与冷峻质感。评论指出其融合了Clan of Xymox、Cold Cave、The Danse Society等经典暗潮元素，整体呈现致敬与继承的姿态。作为暗潮/后朋克领域的作品，其风格与用户偏好高度吻合，但在实验性与跨类型融合方面表现有限，属于暗潮美学框架内的扎实之作。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As if a metronome were forcing its angle further and further outwards...expanding the range until it distorted...the trio, which didn't evoke the image of a trio, begins its second album with "A Visit to Newport Hospital," showcasing organ variations that sound like alarms, red alerts...Dave Stewart combines the magic of the 60s with the mysterious psychedelia that in the 70s would give way to that other Canterbury metric, and Mont Campbell with his measured vocals, plus the organ overlays from which the guiding threads would emerge, the solos of that melody which, as promised at the beginning, were nothing more than alarms of variation on the same note. Jazz and Bossa Nova are implicitly present...staining like raindrops on petals. The alarm awakens us.Contrasong features two tenor saxophones and two trumpets...the monotonous rhythm goes hand in hand with Mont Campbell's singing, and that piano that cuts through Clive Brooks' drums...which cuts through the trumpets...and cuts through the saxophones...and suddenly we're in uncharted territory...like that cover that looks like molten lead, whose solidifying shapes were once used to predict the future... where the trio that did not evoke the image of a trio preferred the mystery of the promise of what it suggests...but is not seen, what is, but is not yet known...an eternal advance, which postpones its realization with the concrete certainty of something that can be heard...can be felt...but not touched, and that when trying to understand it moves away, and comes closer if the mode of perception changes.Boilk is more variations, but in reverse...another way of confirming that intellectual understanding only sets us back...is by not understanding the proposed rules...which are reminiscent of Gy�rgy Ligeti and works like Atmospheres. When, in the final coda, Stewart's other great passion emerges with the Baroque religious organ.Long Piece No. 3 is the album's centerpiece, and here Bach's counterpoints become progressive, slicing through space until they become silence, and then a floating, sidereal space sustained by the drums. Here the trio plays at being a quartet, with the organ's bass lines, leading to an even more ethereal section with the piano...where, from atonal, they could become aggressive, provocative, but always maintaining the tension, that mystery of not knowing what will come next...what note, what chord awaits around the return of the nebula.The second part continues with the variations, the key to the album, creating spacey atmospheres...where that molten lead seems to solidify and take shape...but new suspended melodies, which distanced them from other bands of the genre, anchor them with that Hammond organ with one foot in the 60s, the same as Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother, but firm to the pattern that it is the organ that leads the race, this race without a visible final objective.The third part is considered the most complex, alternating between keyboard and piano, with the piano sections being the most virtuosic and classically accomplished. At times, it recalls the darker segments of Emerson, Lake & Palmer's Pictures at an Exhibition.The fourth and final part is even faster, related to Soft Machine's debut, but the jazzy Bossa rhythm with the keyboard cuts and repetitions, plus the bass and the out-of-tune keyboard, end up distancing it and solidifying this experiment of variations as the triumph of melodic harmony in all its forms.
items._cn_summary: EGG的《The Polite Force》是1971年Canterbury Scene时期的重要作品，展现了该场景独特的器乐实验精神。三重奏配置却呈现出多声部的空间感，融合了爵士即兴、Bossa Nova节奏与Baroque古典元素。评论特别提到与György Ligeti《Atmospheres》等实验古典作品的关联，以及Bach对位法在前卫框架中的运用。器乐编排上大胆突破传统，organ、piano、tenor sax与trumpets形成复杂的对话关系，drums构建出漂浮的太空氛围。专辑在可预测与不可预测之间游走，保持着持续的张力与神秘感。作为七十年代初期的前卫融合尝试，其跨类型融合度与实验性符合用户对实验/前卫及学院派爵士的偏好。

HO CHI MINH CITY: THE OBSERVATORY PRESENTS IRAKLI

Saturday, May 30, 2026

THE OBSERVATORY 26 MAY 2026

Event: The Observatory presents Irakli
Date: Saturday, May 30, 2026
Venue: The Observatory, 85 Cách Mạng Tháng Tám, Bến Thành, Hồ Chí Minh
Line-up: Anna Youth, Irakli, Musleter, Terrace & Tommysarng
Tickets: VND165.000

Tickets available here.

A long one. In the club, Irakli takes over for a rare 5-hour session from 00:00–05:00.

From Tbilisi to Berlin, label head, sound explorer and long-time underground force, Irakli moves fluidly between hypnotic techno, deeper atmospheres and moments that drift somewhere entirely unexpected. Whether stretching into beatless soundscapes or locking into full dancefloor pressure, his sets are patient, immersive and never in a rush.

The long route, properly.

On the terrace, Anna Youth (21:00–00:00) opens with bass-heavy movement, broken rhythms and percussive turns. Tommysarng (00:00–03:00) keeps things rolling — groove-led house and warm late-night energy. Then Musleter (03:00–06:00) takes things into the early hours.

Deep listening inside. Fresh air outside. Clear your schedule for this one.

items._cn_summary: 这场活动聚焦于格鲁吉亚电子音乐人 Irakli 在胡志明市 The Observatory 的深夜演出，呈现催眠 techno 与深层氛围音乐的交融。演出跨越午夜至凌晨五点，时长五小时的沉浸式设置契合用户对电子/实验音乐的偏好。活动同时包含 Anna Youth 的低音驱动节奏、Tommysarng 的 groove 主导 house 以及 Musleter 的凌晨延续，与用户口味中的电子音乐类型高度吻合。作为东欧地下电子场景的代表人物，Irakli 融合实验性与舞池功能性的表演风格，具备一定创新价值。越南作为非主流电子音乐地区，为活动增添地区特色加分。整体而言，这是一场以地下 techno 和氛围电子为核心、面向资深电子乐迷的活动，与用户的实验/电子音乐取向相匹配。

items.excerpt: My Journey with the Silkroad Ensemble “In 2026, I was invited to join the Silkroad Ensemble, the international collective directed by Rhiannon Giddens, as a musician (frame drums, violin, and voice) and contributor of new arrangements and compositions. items.body: Common Ground Beneath Our Feet A Common Ground Beneath Our Feet My Journey with the Silkroad Ensemble In His Own Words: Mauro Durante In 2026, I was invited to join the Silkroad Ensemble, the international collective directed by Rhiannon Giddens, as a musician (frame drums, violin, and voice) and contributor of new arrangements and compositions. Following an initial workshop and preview performance in New York in January 2026, the project will unfold through a North American tour in March 2026, featuring nine concerts alongside workshops and community outreach activities across the United States, as part of the new program Sanctuary: The Power of Resonance and Ritual . The tour will continue later in the year with further residencies and performances in North America and Europe. There are musical projects that are built around a repertoire, others around a geography, and others still around a specific aesthetic vision. The Silkroad Ensemble belongs to a different category: it is a living organism built around an idea. A simple and radical idea at once—that music can be a real space of encounter between cultures, not as a symbolic gesture, but as a daily, concrete, lived practice. Founded in 1998 by Yo-Yo Ma, Silkroad has never been an ensemble in the traditional sense. There is no fixed lineup, no stable repertoire. Instead, it is a community of musicians from different traditions, chosen not only for their technical excellence, but for their ability to inhabit a threshold—the space between rootedness and transformation. Each musician brings with them a language, a sound, a memory. What matters most is the willingness to place that language in dialogue with others, without hierarchy. In recent years, the project has been guided by Rhiannon Giddens, one of the most powerful and deeply insightful voices in contemporary music. Her presence gives the work a clear direction: the goal is not to create an artificial synthesis of traditions, but to create the conditions for each tradition to speak fully, and to transform through encounter. Rhiannon possesses a rare kind of leadership—one that never imposes itself, but quietly shapes the space, both musically and humanly. Entering this context means immediately finding yourself in a space where musical identity is not something to defend, but something to offer. The pizzica, the frame drums, the violin I carry with me are no longer only instruments of a local tradition, but elements in a broader conversation, where every sound is heard both for what it is and for what it might become. It is within this space that my participation in Sanctuary: The Power of Resonance and Ritual began to take shape. Even before the music itself, what stands out is the quality of listening. A real, deep listening, in which every musical gesture is at once personal and collective. This, perhaps, is the true nature of Silkroad: not simply an ensemble, but a place. A circle. A space where music returns to what it has always been—a form of relationship.   Sanctuary: The Power of Resonance and Ritual Music as Refuge and Resistance The word sanctuary can be understood in many ways: refuge, protected space, a place where it is still possible to pause, to listen, to rebuild a sense of community. Working on this project in the United States today carries a particular weight. This is a country marked by deep and increasingly visible tensions, where public discourse is often shaped by fear, by closure, by the idea that identity is something to be defended against someone else. The same tendency can be seen elsewhere—in Italy, across Europe, and in many parts of the world. The rise of nationalism, ongoing wars, and increasingly restrictive migration policies contribute to a climate in which separation begins to feel like the natural order of things. Within this context, finding yourself in a room each day with musicians from Morocco, India, Japan, Armenia, Scotland, Congo, Italy, and the United States becomes something very real. Each person brings their own history, their own sound, their own way of inhabiting music. What emerges is not a fusion of identities, but their coexistence. The taranta, Gnawa music, Indian classical tradition, American folk music—these practices were never conceived merely as forms of entertainment. They were born as tools to accompany moments of transformation, to help individuals and communities move through crisis, grief, healing, and renewal. Sanctuary begins with this understanding. With the idea that music can still be a space where encounter is possible without the need to simplify or protect oneself. A space where listening becomes an act of trust. Something simple and real happens: people from different parts of the world breathe together, listen together, and build something that did not exist before. In a time that often pushes toward division, this act acquires a different weight. It becomes, in its own quiet way, a form of resistance.   Entering the Circle The first rehearsals are always a delicate moment. I took part in an initial workshop in Ireland last December, with a smaller group—Rhiannon, Mazz, Francesco, Niwel, and myself—and then a second workshop with the full ensemble in January, followed by a beautiful preview performance in New York on January 10, 2026, as part of the Winter Jazz Fest. At that stage, there is no shared language yet. You observe each other, you play, you try things, you listen. What strikes you immediately is the extraordinary musical and human level of the people involved. They are incredible. Not only great instrumentalists, but musicians who have developed a deep relationship with their own musical traditions, and who have learned to question them, to keep them flexible and alive. The Hawaiian bassist Shawn Conley, for example, moves effortlessly between bow and pizzicato, shifting from a lyrical, singing tone to remarkable rhythmic agility, using the instrument with a freedom that easily recalls the expressive range of a cello. Beside him, Scottish harpist Maeve Gilchrist brings a presence that is both refined and fearless. Beyond a complete mastery of everything one might expect from the harp—the luminous, almost celestial sound—she possesses an extraordinary rhythmic and harmonic awareness, and a musical curiosity that allows her to make bold, unexpected choices without hesitation. Armenian cellist Karen Ouzounian represents the very highest level of classical tradition, but with something more: a strong personal voice, a deep compositional sensibility, and a lyrical approach to improvisation that makes every gesture feel necessary. With Francesco Turrisi, who like me comes from Italy, we already share a longer history. Yet I remain constantly struck by his ability to move between radically different instruments—accordion, piano, frame drums, string instruments—with complete naturalness. His immense musicality is not tied to any single instrument, but to a broader understanding of sound, form, and structure. Congolese guitarist Niwel Tsumbu is simply one of the finest guitarists I have ever encountered. His relationship with the guitar transcends the instrument itself. He brings together a deep knowledge of African musical traditions, an innate rhythmic sensibility, refined harmonic awareness, and an extraordinary improvisational freedom. Kaoru Watanabe embodies, in a profound way, the idea that tradition is also a choice. Japanese and American, he moves fluidly between cultural languages with a rare balance of respect, discipline, and expressive freedom. His playing is never a reproduction of the past, but its living continuation. With Mehdi Nassouli, on guembri and voice, I feel a particular closeness. Like me with pizzica, he belongs deeply to a specific musical world—in his case, the Gnawa tradition of Morocco. Yet his experience has given him an equally deep ability to engage in dialogue with other musical languages, without ever losing the center of his own sound. Sandeep Das’s presence on tabla is a constant point of reference. He is, quite literally, a guru of Indian music, and yet his authority never creates distance. On the contrary, he makes every interaction feel natural, effortless, both musically and humanly. Japanese percussionist Haruka Fujii brings an extraordinary level of precision and listening. Her virtuosity is never displayed for its own sake, but always placed in service of the music, strengthening the cohesion of the ensemble. American violinist and vocalist Mazz Swift embodies a rare combination of strength and openness. Their voice and violin move fluidly across genres and traditions, grounded yet constantly searching, expanding the expressive space of the group. And then there is Rhiannon. It is difficult to find a single word that captures her presence. She is a complete musician—singer, instrumentalist, composer, dancer, and leader—but above all, she possesses a clarity of vision that holds everything together and inspires everyone around her. Her leadership does not operate through control, but through listening. She creates a space in which each musician can fully express themselves, while contributing to something larger than any individual voice.   Common Ground "Common Ground" is the pizzica I wrote for the Silkroad Ensemble. I use the word “wrote” with caution, because the piece truly exists only through the creative contribution of each musician involved. I laid the foundations: the rhythm, the groove, the structure, the overall architecture, and the fixed melodic and harmonic elements. But what makes it alive is the way each musician inhabits it. The idea first emerged during the workshop in Ireland. At that stage, we were still searching for common ground, a way of being together musically without renouncing our individual identities. It felt natural for me to bring the rhythm of pizzica—my familiar and chosen refuge, my Sanctuary. Back home, I began to develop that intuition, shaping a structure that preserved the physical and rhythmic core of the tradition, while remaining open enough to allow each musician to find their own place within it. We worked on the piece during the workshop in the United States, and performed it live for the first time in New York, just days later, at the Winter Jazz Fest. It was extraordinary to witness how naturally each musician entered that rhythm without hesitation. No one was trying to imitate something that did not belong to them. Instead, each voice emerged clearly, freely coexisting alongside the others. In that moment, I understood that the piece had found its true meaning. It was no longer simply the pizzica I had written, but a shared space. A Common Ground laid beneath our feet. Experiences like this change you in subtle but lasting ways. The energy they transmit, the enthusiasm, the renewed sense of trust in the future—all of it remains. A few years ago, I was in Adelaide to perform at WOMAD with Justin Adams, and the night before our concert I had the chance to attend a performance by Billy Bragg. At one point, he said something that has stayed with me ever since: “Music does not have the power to change the world. But it can make you believe that the world can be changed.” Further information about the Silk Road project This article was originally published in Italian in Blogfoolk Read our review of the latest from Canzionerere Grecanico Salentino
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了Silkroad Ensemble跨文化融合的核心理念，将意大利Puglia地区的pizzica、框架鼓与小提琴等传统元素置于全球化对话语境中。Mauro Durante作为音乐家与编曲者参与其中，强调音乐作为文化交汇空间的实践性，而非刻意的风格融合。Rhiannon Giddens的领导方向明确指向让各传统保持独立表达的同时实现转化。专辑体现了世界音乐与艺术理念创新的结合，但核心仍属于世界音乐范畴，与用户偏好的实验/前卫、爵士、电子类型存在一定距离，更接近跨界融合而非先锋探索。

items.body: Dani Jané - Vida / a RootsWorld review Dani Jané Vida Segell Microscopi Review by Michael Stone V ida , the third release by Dani Jané (Spanish guitar, loops, synthesizer, composition), is a lyrical, rhythmically driven title that combines elements of flamenco, Catalan folk, classical music, jazz, and Catalan and U.S. poetry. A graduate of the Conservatori Superior de Música del Liceu (Barcelona), Jané pursued further study (classical, flamenco, jazz, tango) elsewhere in Spain, and in Germany, France, Italy, and India. Among others, Jané has worked with the flamenco fusion ensemble Tío Montero, flautist Neus Plana Turu, and singers Manuel Araya, Marta Casals, Rusó Sala, and Giulietta Vidal. Marcel Torres (second guitar, effects), Pablo Giménez (transverse flute or side-blown flute, Andean panpipe, percussion), and percussionist Pulmon Beatbox accompany Jané on Vida . Backing the core quartet are flamenco singer Pere Martínez, bassist Tomàs Pujol, and drummer-percussionist Martí Hosta. While studying in Berlín, Jané composed “Preludi” and “El vol de la Vida,” conceived as a classical suite of two movements; about four minutes in, the latter concludes with Martínez’s keening bulerías , with passages from Walt Whitman’s Song of Myself (sung in Spanish-language translation). “Clara” sets up a subtle interplay between Jané’s guitar and Gimenez on flute, over a subdued but insistent bass and percussion foundation. Jané’s grandfather Miquel Castanys wrote the lyrics to “Les penes de l’amor” (the pain of love) in 1938, adapted to a rumba Jané composed during his Berlin sojourn, in tribute to a forebearer Jané knows only through family stories, photos, and his grandfather’s verses. “Lau” presents another guitar-flute encounter accented by understated effects and percussion. Jané composed the instrumental “Milonga C.F. 2.0” with reference to his parents’ home, C.F., i.e., Can Finestres, in the province of Girona, where he spent his early years and first studied with a local guitarist. “Lydda,” a tanguillos by Barcelona’s Toti Soler (whom Jané cites as a major influence), wraps the album, wherein guitar and flute trade licks accented with Carnatic-like vocal percussion. Vida gives voice to a new generation of conservatory trained Catalan artists for whom flamenco is but one among myriad influences. Find the artist online.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自加泰罗尼亚的融合之作，专辑将弗拉门戈、加泰罗尼亚民谣、古典音乐与爵士、电子元素相结合。创作者Dani Jané运用循环吉他、合成器和效果器构建声音层次，并融入惠特曼诗歌西班牙语翻译及祖父1938年歌词等跨文化文本。合作阵容包括长笛、弗拉门戈歌手、beatbox等多元乐器配置。专辑以器乐化和跨界融合为特色，展示了新一代学院派音乐人对传统形式的当代诠释。

items.excerpt: Born in Montreal, Haitian-Canadian musician-composer Jowee Omicil plays a variety of instruments. He came of age in the choral milieu of his father’s Montreal congregation, studied saxophone and music education at Berklee, and has gone on to work with some of the century’s masters. Over the course of 2025, Omicil released one song per month, each accompanied by a philosophizing podcast. The collection is called sMiLes .
items.body: Jowee Omicil - sMiLes / a RootsWorld review Jowee Omicil sMiLes (Bash Village - digital release) Review by Michael Stone sMiLes by Jowee Omicil B orn in Montreal, Haitian-Canadian musician-composer Jowee Omicil plays a fabulous variety of saxophones, clarinets, trumpets, flutes, piano, and keyboards. He came of age in the choral milieu of his father’s Montreal congregation, studied saxophone and music education at Berklee, and gleaned much from engagement with figures including Wyclef Jean, Tony Allen, Ibrahim Maalouf, Roy Hargrove, Kenny Garrett, Pharoah Sanders, Branford Marsalis, and Marcus Miller among others. Over the course of 2025, Omicil released sMiLes one song per month, each accompanied by a philosophizing podcast. The album opens with a striking reinterpretation of singer and Civil Rights activist Abbey Lincoln’s “Throw It Away,” whose message Omicil invokes in his voiceover, an expression of kinship in creative philosophical outlook. (For good measure, Omicil revisits the title on a distinctive “Throw it Away - FuLL oF LoVe Remix.”) Lincoln’s own 2007 rendition on Abbey Sings (Verve) offers critical context, itself worth a comparative audition for the original melody and the contemplative character of her lyrics. Throw it away, throw it away Give your love, live your life, each and every day And keep your hand wide open, let the sun shine through, Because you can never lose a thing, if it belongs to you. In less accomplished hands, the quirky sampling, effects, instrumentation, and wide-ranging, scruffy, sonic bricolage of sMiLes could make for one muddy mélange. But no danger lies here in Jowee’s paradoxical, provocative, sound-shifting extended groove. Omicil's voice and sax blend almost imperceptibly in “SOeuR FeLiX AKA BeeHive.” In “Trip to GHanA,” polyrhythm meets wah-tone high-life guitar, cackly sax, and wordless vocalise. sMiLes by Jowee Omicil sMiLes by Jowee Omicil Feat. Mawuena Kodjovi Other titles transport the listener to Haiti, Morocco, Cape Verde, Jupiter, and Mali. “LeTTre Du MALi PouR JonaTHan” is a meditative, revelatory piano solo nearly ten minutes in length. sMiLes by Jowee Omicil sMiLes may invoke the free-blowing spirit of Miles (as on the sound-effected “MiLes ConvoY”), but there is no anxiety of influence here. Far from a rote genuflection to musical antecedents, the prevailing voice throughout is purely Omicil’s. As he counsels, “trust the note.” "Seek for the sound that is within you and the [instrument] will drive you to your destination… the singularity of sound is what I have always been searching for, the sound that comes from the heart, the sound that maybe, perhaps, is only heard in nature, this is what we are looking for when we are talking about sound… deep down, heartfelt uniqueness, always connected with the spirits…" - Jowee Omicil In accord with his music education formation, Omicil also leads music workshops through his BasH! AkademY, “a close-knit setting embracing spontaneity, authenticity, and shared growth,” which in 2025 included “a nomadic music experience traveling the world” to Mindelo, Cabo Verde. In 2026 Omicil will perform in New York, Canada, Martinique, France, Germany, Austria, Poland, Romania, the UK, and an African tour in the planning stage. Find the artist online.
items._cn_summary: Jowee Omicil的《sMiLes》是一张融合爵士与世界音乐的实验性专辑。这位海地裔加拿大音乐家毕业于伯克利学院，曾与多位爵士和世界音乐大家合作，曲目涵盖采样、效果器、萨克斯与人声的无缝交织，呈现跨越海地、摩洛哥、佛得角、马里乃至木星的多地域音乐图景。专辑采用每月发行一首的独特方式，配合哲学播客，结构上打破传统专辑模式。音乐语汇涉及自由爵士的即兴精神、高Life吉他、复调节奏与人声无词演唱，近乎十分钟的冥想式钢琴独奏展示深厚演奏功底。声音设计带有粗粝的实验质感，但整体统一于Omicil个人化的音乐人格。对照用户偏好的实验、前卫、学院派爵士与世界音乐路线，该专辑契合度较高，是值得关注的跨文化融合之作。

items.body: Lucas Santtana Brasiliano No Format Review by John Alan Urquhart Photo: José de Holanda Brasiliano by Lucas Santtana After nine previous albums and a 25-year career at the forefront of world music, Lucas Santtana is fluent in the many genres of Brazilian music. His new project, Brasiliano , is a musical exploration of the languages of Brazil. With songs sung in Portuguese, French, English, Spanish, Occitan, Cape Verde Creole, and Tupy-Guarani, a Brazilian native language, Santtana has assembled guest lyricists and vocalists representing a range of musical and linguistic influences. The result is a warm and compelling musical treatise on the diverse cultural history of Brazil, expressed through the Brazilian variant of Portuguese, best described as Brasiliano. Returning to his roots, the opening cut and lead single “A história de nossa língua” features Gilberto Gil, a national treasure with whom Santtana worked early in his career. As the liner notes explain, Brasiliano , the language, is depicted in the song as a feminine character meeting other people (languages) on her travels, tracing the history of the language as an offshoot of Latin, including “Occitan, Celtic, Galician, Portuguese, Mozarabic, and others. The chorus features Indigenous words that are part of everyday Brazilian culture: Itapuã, Ipanema, Maracanã, Capoeira, etc.” This song acts as a sort of abstract for the dissertation to follow. Santtana and Gil call and respond over what has become the composer’s trademark mixture of detailed, layered, human-played instruments, including on this track violins and violas, piano, guitars, mellotron, and synths. Throughout the record, Santtana creates an inviting effect with a contemporary gloss, combined with the warm resonance of wood, drum skins, wire strings, sticks, bows, and voices. The album features a range of styles, from the lively party track “Ver meu povo se abraçar” to the convincing reggae of the second single, “Que seja um reggae”. With sophisticated songcraft and inspired arrangements, the songs remain inviting and accessible. Brasiliano by Lucas Santtana Fitting with the theme of the interrelationships among languages, Brasiliano is a celebration of international collaboration. For example, “Independência” features Karyna Gomes, a singer from Guinea-Bissau; Anglo-French performer Piers Faccini sings “Battre des ailes” accompanied by an appropriately French-sounding accordion; and popular Brazilian singer Flavia Coelho is featured on “Dans le sud feat”. The gentle “Strati di tempo” is the closest to Santtana’s earliest singer/guitarist style, with Italian star Dimartino taking the lead vocals. Brasiliano by Lucas Santtana Language is culture; so too are politics. And with the involvement of Gilberto Gill, who served as Minister of Culture in President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government and was jailed and exiled for his political affiliations in the 1960s, it is no surprise that this album is overtly political. For example, on “Línguas Gerais,” French rapper Oxmo Puccino “speaks about colonization.” Continuing to quote from the liner notes, “Indigenous languages and cultures in South America were buried under European colonization.” Tainara Takua and Oxmo Puccino sing “Cocanha” in Occitan. Their music is part of a movement to prevent this endangered romance language from dying out. Like his popular previous recording O Paraíso (2023), which was concerned with the environment, Brasiliano is a concept album that explores the role of linguistics in culture. And like on O Paraíso , Santtana is never preachy. The high-minded intellectual roots of the project are made palatable by the creative and appealing music assembled to tell the story. It is a message of inclusion, collaboration, and the joy of our shared occupancy in this place and at this time. With many languages, many musical styles, and the artistry of many talented and effective musical partners, Brasiliano is a remarkable achievement in curation and musical skill with a compelling contemporary message. items._cn_summary: 巴西音乐人Lucas Santtana的第10张专辑《Brasiliano》是一次跨越多语言与多文化的音乐实验。专辑融合葡萄牙语、法语、英语、西班牙语、奥克语、佛得角克里奥尔语以及巴西本土语言Tupy-Guarani，邀请来自不同国家的音乐人参与合作。音乐层面融合了巴西传统元素、雷鬼节奏、弦乐编排与当代制作，呈现温暖而层次丰富的声响纹理。 Gilberto Gil、Flavia Coelho、Karyna Gomes等嘉宾参与，使专辑兼具政治隐喻与文化 celebration。虽然实验性并非专辑核心，但在世界音乐框架内，其多语言叙事与跨文化协作仍展现出独特的艺术视角，是近年来值得关注的拉丁美洲世界音乐作品。

items.body: Review by alainPP — BRUCE SOORD's 5th album, recorded over 10 years ago, exudes a heightened dreamlike atmosphere, based on acoustic sounds, reflecting his past life like a musical epitaph."Concepcion" opens with an acoustic guitar riff, a melancholic Southern lament, an evening in Chile, a heartfelt cry for his mother giving birth. "Meet Me on the Downs" is a mid-tempo ballad with his voice as the instrument, a slow, ethereal, decrescendoing sound reminiscent of the end of a concert in Hamburg. "Pillars," with its melody etched into our musical subconscious, features a slide guitar that shines, illuminates, and opens the mind. It evokes the feeling of a Western ballad, riding these reverberating notes, rich like a cactus at sunset, where the heat makes the air vibrate. A beautiful melody dealing with excessive introspection, the quest for balance, a reference to Saint Simeon Stylite. "You Made a Promise," with its prominent, almost oppressive acoustic guitar over a pastoral choir, and a raw, crystalline vocal delivery, all in under three minutes. "Our Predicament" features lingering guitar notes and metronomic sixteenth notes amplifying the contemplative sound. The off-kilter vocals heighten the impression of a solitary lament. The electric guitar solo evokes the plaintive post-rock of KWOON, an intimate moment you wouldn't want to share with your horse at dusk. "Day of Wrath" shifts gears, repetitive from the start, reminiscent of Mariusz's work on LUNATIC SOUL. A catchy, addictive sound, and then Bruce launches into an airy, pastoral, uplifting ballad where the metronomic feel allows you to escape the torpor induced at the beginning of the album. A musical surge, ambient with an encroaching synth, the album truly takes off with this sound reminiscent of PINEAPPLE THIEF, a return to their roots. "Stared Down" returns to its primal acoustic roots, its latent intimacy lingering on post-rock undertones, reminiscent of ANATHEMA, with that famous, soaring guitar solo."Kept Me Thinking," the creaking of a chair on the side of a house in Louisiana, is the first of two long tracks; I was getting impatient. Note the contribution of Jon, a PINEAPPLE THIEF collaborator, on bass for this crescendoing track that flows like a drink in the middle of the desert. Easy melody, vocals, and a melancholic guitar worthy of Brother CAVANAGH. A track that reminds us that you don't need a whole fleet of instruments to be great. The final solo screams with joy, lets loose, and feels good; an oriental-tinged choral finale. "Ghosts in the Park" begins with a meandering acoustic guitar, the other a plaintive electric ballad typical of PINEAPPLE THIEF?old habits die hard. A suspended 1'45" intro, and you think it's over; and then, and then the air begins to move, tickling our ears, leaving us to search for the musical direction, the Oberhausen creative space. The essence of the progressive spirit is evident in the minimalist drums accompanying these radiant post-acoustic guitar notes, letting the ear wander for a long time, taking its time. The finale seems to settle at the 10-minute mark, but then comes the organic shift, a fragile, latent sound, a musical spiderweb drawing the listener into Bruce's very room, listening to him strum and hum this last fleeting, archaic, ephemeral melody.Bruce Soord has given himself up without musical artifice; emotion, restraint, intimacy, and sincerity define this stripping bare with his acoustic guitar.
items._cn_summary: 这是布鲁斯·索德2026年的跨界前卫摇滚专辑，历经十年沉淀。专辑以原声吉他为核心，融合后摇、民谣与渐进摇滚元素，呈现出梦幻而内省的音乐氛围。曲目如"Pillars"和"Kept Me Thinking"展现了他标志性的旋律构建能力，其中"Kept Me Thinking"融入东方合唱元素，呈现独特的文化融合视角。整张专辑以Pineapple Thief式的氛围营造和Anathema式的情感张力为基调，在传统渐进摇滚框架内融入了世界音乐色彩。作为小众独立发行，专辑在实验性和跨界融合上有一定追求，但核心仍属于摇滚范畴，与用户偏好的纯实验、电子或爵士路线存在一定距离。
