items.body: Review by The Progolyte — I had heard rumors in the community about this record being an underrated gem of the Rock Progressivo Italiano scene, so today I finally check it out. The record is called Flore Di Metallo by I Califfi, and overall I got some really nice vibes from this one. While it may not be top-tier in the world of Italian prog, it's got some really nice keyboard-based rock music with a nice twinge of excitement oozing out of it. The cover didn't seem to convey the musical identity that much, with the more moody atmosphere I got from it, but that part of this album was still pretty good as well. Moving on, I really enjoyed the musicianship and thought the personnel had a lot of talent being the classic four-man crew. It includes Sandro Cinotti on keyboards, Vincenzo Amadei on guitar, Franco Boldrini on bass, Maurizio Boldrini on drums, and then all but Sandro helps out with the vocals. The music is quite strong, having an ear-catching mix of hard rock and symphonic prog. You also get some acoustic bits on songs like Alleluia and Felicit�, Sorriso E Pianto, which seem to fit in as a counter to the much more erratic styles on other pieces. The songs do seem to be a little shorter than what I would like, but the material here is strong enough to make up for the lacking lengths. These guys sound very similar to Quella Vecchia Locanda at points, specifically the more rock-focused bits of their debut album, though they still have those classical elements floating around here and there. Tracks like Flore Finto, Flore Di Metallo, and Varius are some of the most exciting, bombastic, and interesting compositions on the album. They approach heavy jazz fusion and avant prog at points while also playing into more somber and moody tones. Other highlights on the album include the opener Nel Mio Passato and Campane, which have some really nice depth along with beginning and ending the record nicely. In conclusion, I enjoyed this one quite a bit, and I'll definitely be coming back to it more often. It's incredibly engaging with the listener and always delving deep into the musical environment of the fusions of heavy psych and wild symphonic prog, and I hope more people listen to this one soon enough. As for my final rating, I think I'll go with a mid or strong 4/5.
items._cn_summary: 这张1973年的意大利前卫摇滚专辑融合了硬摇滚、交响前卫与爵士融合元素，展现出键盘主导的强劲演奏风格与实验性尝试。评论者特别提及的“heavy jazz fusion and avant prog”表明专辑具有跨类型融合特征，且包含原声段落等多样化编排。四人乐队的演奏功底扎实，作品在情绪表达上兼具张力和深度。作为意大利前卫摇滚场景中的作品，其文化背景具有一定特色，但意大利在欧洲音乐版图中并不属于非主流地区。专辑长度偏短是唯一被指出的不足。对于偏好实验/前卫爵士融合的听众而言，这张作品具有吸引力，但硬摇滚基底使其与纯实验或暗潮路线存在距离。

items.body: Here, he stands swallowed by the sky Life, so small – dust in nature’s eye He seeds the ground, fallow by death’s hand Our hidden past, the fiction of all man L’Avenir has ushered in their latest album, Secrets, with the video for Animism, a coldwave séance of mineral calm and occult motion, where the air seems to have been left under overnight under a full moon, and returned with new intelligence. The Baltimore project, led by Jason Sloan, treats electronic music as architecture as much as emotion: a corridor of blue light, a stairwell descending beneath memory, a voice arriving from somewhere just beyond the visible wall. On this first single from the project’s eighth album, Sloan works with a familiar vocabulary: patient drum-machine pressure, icy synthesizers, distant singing – but the result feels newly charged, as if each element has been placed glowing under glass. Animism takes its title with admirable seriousness. The song imagines a world in which matter has memory and the inanimate keeps counsel. The earth, the tree, the old room, the object handled too often by human longing: all seem to possess a private pulse. Sloan’s voice sits inside the track rather than above it, less a guide than a presence caught in the same current as the listener. The effect is intimate and estranged, the sound of someone speaking from within a thought that has become physical. The track brings to mind the elegant austerity of Eleven Pond, the dusky romanticism of Clan of Xymox, the severe European mechanics of Parade Ground, and the cerebral chill of Trisomie 21. These references move through the song like figures glimpsed in frosted glass, recognizable but never allowed to dominate the room. The arrangement advances with a measured hand, giving each synth line and percussive motion enough space to breathe before the next cold gleam arrives. The accompanying video, directed by Soleil Noir Studios, deepens the spell. Shot by Jason Sloan, with Sloan also handling video synthesizer programming and both analogue and digital hardware, the clip turns the forests of the mind into a prismatic terrain. Bright colours bloom against mirrored images; faces and forms double, dissolve, and reassemble in a kind of psychic woodland. The imagery suggests a psychedelic passage through inner nature, where branches become nerves, light becomes thought, and perception starts to behave like a living organism. Animism presents L’Avenir as a project still devoted to solitude, mystery, and nocturnal design, but newly attentive to the strange life hidden inside surfaces. Sloan makes darkwave feel porous here, open to trees, stones, ghosts, and the quiet intelligence of everything we mistakenly believe is still. items.body: We are asking the questions, we are lying to get by We are lying on our backs, wondering about the sky We are blind when it suits us, we still hear the noise Are these delusions of our making? Is this the illusion of choice? Every life eventually arrives at the same locked door: the one behind which the meaning of it all is supposed to be waiting. As the years burn, we gather love, pleasure, machines, money, memories, and little mementos of our existence, only to find the old questions still standing there, untouched, and unanswered. With “All We’ve Known of Heaven,” Soft Vein turns that existential ache into a sleek new wave confession, one lit by bright synths, bruised romance, and the uneasy knowledge that abundance does not always equal salvation. The second single from his forthcoming new album continues Justin Chamberlain’s recent evolution into a more refined, sophisticated synthpop silhouette. Where earlier Soft Vein material often leaned heavily into darkwave gloom, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” moves with a more cinematic sense of yearning: a sighing, almost church-like introduction that opens into a pulsing bass synth, rippling electronics, and a breathy vocal performance that feels suspended between confessions. The song follows the previously released single Chekov in placing Chamberlain’s voice and songwriting front and center. Co-produced by Chamberlain with Andrea Mantione of Nuovo Testamento, the track has the sheen of expensive glass and the anxiety of someone staring straight through it. There is an unmistakable 1980s charge here: a nocturnal, Michael Mann-like glow; the elegant propulsion of new wave pop; and vocal harmonies that call to mind the grand emotional sweep of Simple Minds without slipping into too much of their new gold sheen. Lyrically, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” circles the elegant catastrophes of modern life: desire, consumption, spiritual exhaustion, and the little betrayals people commit simply to keep moving. Soft Vein writes about a world in which modern convenience has multiplied beyond imagination — machines for pleasure, endless means of contact, every comfort summoned on command — yet we seem no closer to one another, and no nearer to knowing anything like heaven. The song asks what remains when everything has been acquired except meaning, understanding excess as both seduction and trap: the comfort that dulls us, the desire that divides us, and the search for warmth in the wrong rooms. The song’s central question — “Is this all we are?” — becomes less a cry of defeat than a flare sent into the cogs of our disconnected digital existence, in search of a sign of life beyond our modern illusions. And by the time Rachel Mazer’s saxophone arrives near the finale, it feels like that signal briefly answered: romantic, wounded, and gone almost as soon as it appears. Listen to “All We’ve Known of Heaven” below: All We’ve Known of Heaven by SOFT VEIN Mastered by Jason Corbett of ACTORS, “All We’ve Known of Heaven” suggests Soft Vein is expanding in real time, stepping further into an 80s pop architecture while keeping a darkwave pulse beating beneath the floorboards. There is a compelling parallel in Producer Phil Thornalley’s own arc, from the Gothic depths of The Cure’s Pornography era to the gleaming new wave heights of Johnny Hates Jazz. For Soft Vein, that kind of range does not feel like a contradiction or retreat, but the natural continuum of any good artist: a movement from severity to sophistication, from dread to desire, from the basement to the bright lights without losing the ache underneath. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Conceived during the tour for the previous album, Led Zeppelin's second volume is so distinct that it possesses its own autonomy. The approach is more direct, the sound is rawer, the songs seem tailor-made for live performance, and Page's growth as a riff-maker, one of his many facets, encompassing hard rock, blues, and soul, is gradually evident. However, certain litanies, remnants of psychedelia, can detract somewhat from the effectiveness, diverting the focus, as can be seen in "Whole Lotta Love" or "Moby Dick." These disruptions might be justifiable in a live performance, but in the studio version, they diminished the impact of gems that otherwise would have shone even brighter. Beyond this compositional observation, the band was at the height of its creative powers, brimming with ideas, and each member contributing their own unique touch.What Is and What Should Never Be breaks new ground, with jazzy undertones and a fusion of 60s British pop, blues, and funk... all within a song format, with Jimmy Page knowing when to glide peacefully and when to attack with deadly ferocity.Throughout Volume II, John Paul Jones's presence grows enormously, underpinning the foundations of the tracks until he becomes indispensable. Robert Plant had already developed his own style, making his voice another instrument and another flagship of the quartet's sound.The Lemon Song continues as a fundamental building block in what is constructed on this second album, where if it teaches us one lesson, it's that the blues is always something more, a vehicle to add elements and enrich the journey. And John Paul Jones's bass, which one can hear at times in addition to Jimmy's guitar, and the groove achieved were limitless.Led Zeppelin was always more than just good music. Unlike other bands on their contemporaries with similar characteristics, a certain mystical air gradually awakened within them, particularly in Jimmy Page, and that aura was transferred to compositions like "Thank You," music by Page and lyrics by Plant, an instant classic, almost like entering a chapel with muddy boots...guided by John Paul Jones' organ, before returning to the plea in "Heartbreaker," and another immortal guitar riff (not many can say the same). And fundamentally, there was that communion of the group, whose chemistry was at its best, those years when they were like an indivisible unit...recording together, traveling together, eating together, and that translated into the music.With "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)," they do whatever they want with time and rhythm, constantly changing them, making the song another example of instantaneous change within a song format, stretching and forever altering it. "Ramble On" will be a first approach to that electro-acoustic format that they will fully explore in Volume III, with Plant dressed in one of his many guises, and again the bass roving alongside the guitar, driving the rhythm of the composition. A funky, groovy drum rhythm that becomes Andean-like with guitars on the cliffs, with Page already playing his intricate parts that nevertheless seem simply enchanting in their placidity. And therein lies its charm!They could explode...and they could curl up in a corner...Bring It On Home closes a bluesy album full of contrasts, trying out different outfits and sharpening their weapons for the future...everything was here waiting for the moment to be used...but masters of the stage...lighting only what they wanted to be seen...the quintessence of a band that covered ground with an aerial perspective.
items._cn_summary: 《Led Zeppelin II》是1969年发行的经典硬摇滚/布鲁斯摇滚专辑，由英国乐队Led Zeppelin演绎。专辑以强劲的吉他riff驱动，融合了布鲁斯、灵魂乐和早期迷幻摇滚元素。Jimmy Page的吉他演奏在这张专辑中展现出显著成长，Robert Plant已形成独特的演唱风格，John Paul Jones的贝斯和键盘编排为作品提供了坚实的根基。乐评指出部分歌曲中的迷幻残余段落略显冗长，但整体上乐队处于创作力的巅峰期，多首曲目如《What Is and What Should Never Be》和《Ramble On》展现出音乐形式的灵活变化能力。作为老牌经典摇滚乐队作品，该专辑与用户偏好（实验/前卫、爵士、电子等）匹配度较低，但在摇滚乐历史语境中具有重要的创新意义和艺术价值。

items.body: Review by TenYearsAfter — Ruud Dielen had a long history with cover bands , playing guitar in songs from Jimi Hendrix, Santana, Led Zeppelin, Queen, Toto and Genesis. After many years touring in the more commercial circuit, he decided that it was time to write his own music and in 2017 he produced his first album entitled Aquarius, as a one-man-band (guitar, bass and synthesizers), under the name Glorious Wolf. The music sounds as a tribute to the Seventies era progrock and Classic Rock, from Pink Floyd to Zappa and Hendrix, embellished with a wonderful array of vintage sounds (from Moog, Mellotron and Hammond to Gibson, Fender and Mesa Boogie). On his second album Zodiac (2019) and third Mysterious Traveller (2023) Ruud started to invite male and female singers, and to blend the progrock sound with a more song-oriented and varied musical attitude. On Prog Archives Ruud Dielen his Glorious Wolf project got a lot of praise for that musical formula, meandering tastefully and elaborately between instrumental Old School vintage keyboard drenched progrock and song-oriented tracks. And now, anno 2026, here's Ruud again (playing acoustic - and electric guitars, fretless bass, Precision bass, synthesizers, mellotron and FX drums) with Glorious Wolf, featuring a range of national and international guest musicians, on vocals, drums, bass, Hammond, Yamaha piano, Mellotron, theremin and saxophone. Most of the foreign musicians Ruud had met during an international musical collaboration.Elements of Hope Pt.1 ? Instrumental (4.34) : This new album starts with an exciting electronic music atmosphere featuring pulsating sequencers and spacey synthesizers, then howling and biting Gilmourian guitar runs, topped with Mellotron choirs, followed by a tight and catchy beat. The music is embellished with Ruud his powerful guitar runs, fat synthesizer flights and soaring Mellotron choirs, and backed by a fluent rhythm-section (Kike Paglia on drums and Tim Ros on bass). In the end majectic Mellotron choirs erupt, wow, what an impressive start!Elements of Hope Pt.2 - Carrying this Yoke (6.15) : The intro delivers psychedelic sounding Mellotron violins. The music turns into a folky climate with acoustic guitar and fragile English male vocals (by Frank van der Borg), in a slow rhythm. Gradually a more lush sound featuring Mellotron violins, and powerful vocals and guitar riffs. In the final part a break with raw guitar riffs and propulsive drum beats. Lots of contrast, variety and dynamics, and tastefully arranged.Elements of Hope Pt.3 - Into the Clouds (5.55) : First celestial female vocals (by Jyoti Verhoeff) and twanging acoustic guitar, in a dreamy and hypnotizing climate, wonderful. Now the sound becomes more lush, embellished with fretless bass, slow drumbeats and distinctive female vocals. Gradually the atmosphere is working to a symptuous climax with a synthesizer solo, powerful drums and Hammond, culminating into fiery guitar solo, how exciting.Elements of Hope Pt.4 ? Instrumental (1.42) : A short piece in an ominous climate, with raw and powerful guitar, and slow and powerful drumbeats, the interplay is awesome.Elements of Hope Pt.5 - Life's Chaotic Spell (5.51) : The final part of this 5-pieve epic title track contains omnipresent Hammond, blended with exciting rock guitar, powerful male English vocals and a propulsive rhythm-section. Now saxophone play (by Reg Parham) joins, strongly coloring the music, with hints from Frank Zappa and King Crimson. Finally a heavy guitar solo, backed by a dynamic rhythm-section and Hammond.If You Please ? instrumental (6.20) : This composition delivers a slow rhythm and a compelling climate, Ruud really shines with his guitarwork, from sensitive to fiery, and using the tremolo-arm and wah-wah pedal, prog meets bluesrock, wow. Halfway beeps and bleeps, then a more atmospheric sound featuring spectacular wah-wah driven guitar runs, backed by propulsive drumbeats.If I Only (5.46) : After an intro with Mellotron (by the late Thomas Zunk) and militairy drums the music turns into a slow rhythm with heavy guitar, strong male vocals and gradually a more bombastic atmosphere. Halfway a fiery guitar solo, with howling and biting leads and Hammond layers, the music builds and builds, very compelling and exciting.Whirlwinds & Maelstroms ? instrumental (6.44) : Another Mellotron soaken intro, then slow drumbeats and powerful guitar. Halfway a swirling Hammond solo (XK5 Hammond with Leslie by Harry Knapen), followed by a heavy guitar solo, the interplay is excellent.Everything Must Break to Grow - EoH Pt.2 Reprise (6.25) : The final track on this new album starts with dreamy piano and vocals, then a slow rhythm, in a melancholical atmosphere, topped with subtle slide guitar. Gradually the sound turns into more lush and powerful featuring rock guitar and a dynamic rhythm-section. Finally dreamy with spacey synthesizers, guitar and voices, another example of Ruud his interesting and varied musical ideas.In the 3 years after his previous effort Ruud has moved and built a high-tec studio in his new home. You can hear the result: a mature and elaborate new album on which the music is wonderfully meandering between Old School prog and a more varied and song-oriented musical approach, embellished with his awesome guitarwork, vintage keyboards and vocal leads, and backed by good musicians. After Edo Spanninga (as E.D.O.) with his solo album The Past Is A Foreign Country, his other project Trion with Terra Tiempo here is another excellent new Dutch prog effort, well done Ruud!
items._cn_summary: 这是一张受七十年代复古前卫摇滚影响的跨界专辑，融合了Pink Floyd、Zappa和Hendrix等经典元素，同时引入sequencer、spacey synth等电子音乐声响，并运用Mellotron、Moog、Hammond等复古键盘音色。专辑在传统prog rock与song-oriented tracks之间游走，增添了迷幻氛围和丰富的动态变化。虽有复古致敬倾向，但编曲考究且融合了电子与古典摇滚元素，对于偏好实验前卫音乐的用户来说，具有一定的跨界融合价值和创新意义。

items._cn_summary: 1976年Paul Bley、John Gilmore、Jimmy Giuffre三位自由爵士先驱的专辑重评。Bley作为加拿大实验爵士钢琴家，其自创厂牌的首批发行具有音乐史意义。Giuffre以中音萨克斯和单簧管探索自由即兴边界，Gilmore则带来Coltrane式精神性维度。三人合作代表了70年代自由爵士的成熟阶段，融合即兴深度与结构探索。评论援引Roger Dean的音乐学视角，肯定了Bley在自由爵士运动中的实验精神与厂牌建设贡献。专辑体现了学院派爵士与实验性的结合，适合偏好自由爵士与即兴传统的听众。内容为五十年回顾性评价，信息量有限但具史料价值。

items.body: Mats Edén    Tellef Kvifte Knut Kvifte Nesheim Króta Taragot Review by Mike Adcock Króta by Edén/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Króta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Edén has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sjøfløyte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Króta by Edén/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with “Fossgrimen,” a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Króta by Edén/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish “Polska from Per Myhr,” having played a repeated introductory riff on the sjøfløyte, with Mats Edén providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Edén who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt. Króta by Edén/Kvifte/Nesheim trio From the title of "Springar from Knut Nord-Juveli" we learn that it was taken from the repertoire of a renowned sjøfløyte player from Numedal, a valley in the east of Norway and is an appropriate feature for Tellef Kvifte. A springar is a Norwegian triple-beat dance whose three beats vary in length depending on which region of Norway the tune comes from. In this case the underlying pulse resembles that of a rhumba with each bar having two similar beats followed by a shorter one; but the melodic structure is unmistakably Norwegian with a motif being repeated, then the third time through it developing into a variation. Króta by Edén/Kvifte/Nesheim trio “På Siljan“ was taken from a collection of old Swedish tunes, but the version here is not so much an interpretation as a deconstruction of an item from the Swedish fiddle tradition. Beginning with Edén playing freely, seeking out the resonances of the fiddle through the gentle scraping of the strings with the bow, the tune eventually arrives quietly through the back door, carried by Kvifte on his sjøfløyte while Edén continues to improvise, along with Nesheim playing loosely around his kit. Tellef Kvifte pretty much sticks to the tune, a thread that runs through the track while the other two work around it, creating a rich sound texture, the listener being challenged to decide which is in front and which is behind. An adventurous and worthwhile endeavour which shows once again how traditional music can be not merely a legacy to uphold, but a catalyst for creativity. Find the artists online. Mats Edén Tellef Kvifte Knut Kvifte Nesheim Further reading: Groupa - Kind Of Folk Volume 2: Norway Guro Kvifte Nesheim and Floating Sofa Quartet - Kystnært Tellef Kvifte - The Norwegian Bagpipe (?) items._cn_summary: 这张由瑞典小提琴手Mats Edén与挪威笛子演奏家Tellef Kvifte及其子Knut Kvifte Nesheim组成的三重奏专辑，对北欧传统曲目进行了远离常规的演绎。评论指出其音乐质感更接近室内乐，三位演奏者之间呈现亲密的对话式交流。专辑有意识地探索民间音乐中隐藏的神秘感与黑暗面向，如以传说中的瀑布精灵为灵感的开场曲目。然而整体仍建立在传统民谣框架之上，虽有创新意图但实验性表达相对有限，融合力度不足以获得更高评分。

items.body: Neba Solo and Benego Diakité - A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking / a RootsWorld review Neba Solo and Benego Diakité A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking Nonesuch Review by Mike Adcock Photo: Aboubacar Traoré A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking by Neba Solo & Benego Diakité The newly released album from Malian musicians Neba Solo and Benego Diakité is the outcome of a project which began in 2013 when Solo and Diakité, playing balafon and n'goni respectively, were recorded by Bamako producer Ousmane Haïdara. He played the result to another record producer, Nick Gold, who was completely taken by what he heard and together they decided to work on the recording to produce a finished album, also enlisting English musician Sonny Johns to help with the production. Gold had previously brought together Ali Farka Touré and Toumani Diabaté to record what was to become the very successful album In the Heart of the Moon and this was a similar story, Solo and Diakité also being established Malian musicians coming from different musical backgrounds. Indeed, the balafon and n'goni, though both widely associated with Malian music, are seldom played together. A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking , released as a double CD, is very much an album of two halves. The recordings made in 2013 of the two musicians playing together were transformed over time into ensemble arrangements with the addition of other musicians playing strings, mellotron, guitar and percussion, plus overdubbed vocals from Solo and three female singers. These reworked tracks make up the first half of the album. A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking by Neba Solo & Benego Diakité The opening track, “Djinê Mogo Tiki” begins with a capella backing vocals before Diakité introduces a repeated riff on the n'goni over which Solo improvises on the balafon while also taking the lead vocal, a pattern which forms the basis of all the tracks, with the augmented instrumentation creating further layers of interest. “Djinê Mogo Tiki” is one of two tracks to have strings added and these sit well, used sparingly to provide short rhythmic motifs, thankfully belying any fears that might be raised by mention of a string arrangement. A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking by Neba Solo & Benego Diakité The reinvention of these pieces, clearly done with the co-operation of both Solo and Diakité, may be radical but it has nevertheless been carried out with consideration and musical sensibility. “Yeredon Bali” begins with a few phrases from Solo's balafon, to be joined by Diakité's n'goni, some light percussion and hand claps and then more of the female backing vocals, supporting Solo's vocal in the call and response style characteristic of so much Mande music. In this case the vocal content is the only significant addition to the original duo recording, but significant it is because, in the nature of things, once a vocal line is added that becomes the main focus of attention. What makes the format of this album particularly intriguing is that the final six tracks give us the opportunity of hearing the original, unadorned versions of most of the arranged tracks as first recorded by Neba Solo and Benego Diakité. They are referred to as the “Garden Demos” since they were recorded in a Bamako garden under a mango tree. Without the added vocals the focus shifts to the interplay between the two musicians, and the meaning of the music changes. "Djine Mogo Tiki (Garden Demo excerpt) For example, we are offered two versions of "Djinê Mogo Tiki," first appearing as the album's opening track in its arranged version, then later in the original duo take. Perhaps this has been done to show two sides of the same story, with an awareness too of differences in what audiences are looking for. The arranged tracks, with their instrumental variety and vocal additions, certainly work well and might help give the music wider appeal. But if you are someone who is captivated by listening to fine players engaged in a musical conversation, eavesdropping on the almost telepathic interaction taking place as the two musicians explore the common ground between them, then it's really already there in the earlier Garden Demos, the final six tracks of A Djinn and a Hunter Went Walking . items._cn_summary: 来自Mali的两位音乐家内巴·索洛与贝内戈·贾基特的合作专辑，展现非洲曼丁音乐中罕见的balafon与n'goni对话。项目始于2013年的二重奏录音，后经制作人尼克·戈尔德等人编排为带弦乐、mellotron和女声合唱的完整合奏作品。专辑保留传统旋律框架同时融入当代制作元素，是非洲传统与世界音乐融合的有趣尝试。发行厂牌Nonesuch，属于独立唱片体系中的主流世界音乐系列，符合用户对世界音乐的关注偏好，但实验性和创新性相对有限，整体偏向传统与现代的稳健融合。

items.excerpt: This collaboration between the five-piece Belgian instrumental group Wör , whose members specialize in bringing the music of earlier centuries to life, and Kongero , the acclaimed Swedish female a capella folk quartet, offers an unusual chance to explore how their two cultures, ostensibly so different, can come together. It might sound an unlikely mix, but here’s a spoiler: it turns out they’re pretty much musical best friends.
items.body: WÖR x Kongero - Songbooks Live / a RootsWorld review WÖR x Kongero Songbooks Live Review by Chris Nickson WÖR, Kongero - Songbooks Live by Nordic Notes This collaboration between the five-piece Belgian instrumental group Wör, whose members specialize in bringing the music of earlier centuries to life, and Kongero, the acclaimed Swedish female acapella folk quartet, offers an unusual chance to explore how their two cultures, ostensibly so different, can come together. It might sounds an unlikely mix, but here’s a spoiler: it turns out they’re pretty much musical best friends. The album kicks off at a cracking pace with “Var Är Du?”, a bravura performance through a twisted, tortuous piece that manages to be both elegant and surprising. However, the true astonishment arrives at the end, when the audience applauds and you suddenly realize this was recorded live (actually over two separate performances). WÖR, Kongero - Songbooks Live by Nordic Notes The musicians bring material from their separate traditions, plus one original, showcasing their skills in intricate, swinging arrangements for both instruments and voices. Thanks to their skill, the varied ideas fit together seamlessly so it’s brimming with delights, like the wonderfully-titled “Drinking Like A Sweet Swede,” where the singers layers their harmonies over a jaunty backing. Everything is intricate, performed with a glowing precision that can disarm the senses with its beauty. The highlight, perhaps, is the beautiful “Klosterjungfrun.” The slow, seductive opening draws in the listener, the voices airy and light, curling around each other as the instruments wind long their path their. It’s a beautiful piece, but really, just one gem among so many here. WÖR, Kongero - Songbooks Live by Nordic Notes There’s never a foot wrong, no note out of place and the performances are passionate, stellar, a true collaboration of instruments and voices. Add to that a mix that’s sharp as a razor, and Songbooks Live is a truly outstanding album, a perfect illustration that people have more in common than separates them. And it illustrates exactly what artists can achieve live. With luck, they’ll work together again. Soon, please. Find the artists online. items._cn_summary: 这是一张比利时WÖR乐团与瑞典Kongero女声四重奏的现场合作专辑，融合北欧民谣声乐与欧洲古典器乐传统。专辑收录两场不同演出录音，曲目涵盖各自传统曲目及一首原创作品，编曲精致讲究，声乐层次丰富，器乐伴奏灵动如“Drinking Like A Sweet Swede”等曲目展现出跨界协作的默契。现场录音捕捉到自然的声场与观众互动。作为小众独立厂牌Nordic Notes发行，专辑体现了欧洲民间与古典音乐的文化交汇，整体品质扎实，但创新性与实验性有限，更适合对世界民谣及古典器乐融合有兴趣的听众，而非追求激进实验或前卫突破的听众。

items.body:
Callum Au is not one for half measures. As an arranger he has worked with international orchestras and contributed to movie scores; as a performer he is an in-demand session trombonist. He steps into the spotlight with Sing Seven Seas, a project of genuinely epic ambition: 81 musicians, a voiceover artist, 16 compositions and nearly two hours of music. The album explores classic swing, progressive orchestral arrangements and contemporary jazz, with Au contributing trombone alongside a remarkable cast of cross-generational talent.

While conceived as a single project, the music falls into two volumes, the first highlights Au's compositions across a variety of styles, the second draws on the big band tradition and pays tribute to his influences.

Opening track: "Swipe Right!" is intended to capture the age of Instagram and TikTok but conjures up the atmosphere of the 1920s rather than the 2020s. Nonetheless, Au's arrangement is fluid and tight, the trombone cascade delights and Duncan Hemstock adds a terrific clarinet solo—leaving you with a broad smile regardless of the decade.

Jake Wilson's electric guitar and Nadim Teimoori's tenor saxophone are the clear highlights cutting through the dense structure of "Galt's Motor." "Si Vis Pacem Para Carnyx," a nod to the Iron Age Celtic wind instrument, opens in cinematic orchestral fashion before the focus shifts to a traditional folk band, but the two worlds never convincingly merge or complement each other, with the track stretching on longer than the idea can sustain.

Au's skills as an arranger and trombonist shine on "Murmurations," making it one of the album's highlights. Equally enjoyable is "The Weaver," where the lilting melody gives Teimoori another opportunity to impress. "Jazz AI" is a terrific romp in which artificial intelligence runs amok at a conservatoire. Kate Emmerton's words, narrated by Matt Forbes, set the scene for Au's trombone, Emma Rawicz's tenor saxophone and James Davison's flugelhorn to contribute brilliantly to the mayhem.

Au seems more at home on the second volume, drawing on the influences of Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Kenny Wheeler and others who have shaped his musical voice. The big band blast of "Bandwagon Blues" swings with swagger, driven by solo exchanges and shifting ensemble combinations. Jointly composed by Au and his son, "Through The Deep Dark Woods" is inventive and playful, while the Latin rhythms of "Caledonian Sun God" bring out excellent contributions from pianist Rob Barron and trumpeter Ryan Quigley.

The ensemble are on top of their game all through the recording, as are all the principal soloists, with Freddie Gavita's flugelhorn and Martin Williams' tenor saxophone showcased on "Fork Hen" and Simon Marsh's alto saxophone a feature on "Verity."
items._cn_summary: 这是一张81人编制的英国爵士大乐队专辑，分两卷呈现。第一卷展示创作者在不同风格间的探索，包含复古摇摆、电影配乐式管弦乐以及人工智能主题的当代爵士作品；第二卷则致敬埃灵顿、贝西伯爵等传统大师，以拉丁节奏和经典大乐队语汇为主导。专辑亮点在于精良的管弦乐编曲、高水平的独奏演绎以及跨世代音乐家阵容。部分曲目如凯尔特元素作品存在风格融合不够自然的问题。整体而言属于学院派爵士范畴内的扎实之作，融合了部分实验性元素但仍以传统爵士语言为核心，与用户偏好的实验/前卫和暗潮风格距离较远。

items.body: Review by alainPP — "The Silent Architect" features an organic rhythm followed by a groove worthy of Dream Theater, a metal riff with a "Kashmir-like" feel, and a melodic battleground. Nathan's voice dazzles over a heavy prog riff reminiscent of Kamelot, for example. The guitar solo and other solos drive the frenetic rhythm and instrumental onslaught, all power metal. "Doors of Yesterday" is a melancholic ballad highlighted by Dean's piano, with a saccharine classical orchestration over a pop melody oozing emotion, its metallic riff subtly present in the background. It evokes fond memories of the 80s, a time when quality reigned supreme. "The Invisible Countdown" boasts a distinctive vocal style, a reminiscent of Vanden Plas's prog metal DNA, and a wild, heavy riff. The catchy, mainstream heavy rock melody features a sharp guitar solo and an orchestration approaching the valiant Fates Warning. The final fade-out is somewhat redundant, however. "Mr. Crazy" breaks the mold, offering the raw, frenetic, and compulsive hard rock of their earlier work, with Nathan sounding more like Aerosmith. A punk-infused track with a colossal drumbeat, perfect for some serious headbanging. "Arrow" is the second, more mainstream, mid-tempo ballad, soothing on acoustic guitar and filled with backing vocals from Nathan and Dean. The irresistible melody makes you want to sing along to the chorus, shoulders intertwined; it's 80s rock boosted by today's powerful sound."Dust & Bone" kicks off again, like a heavy machine gun, the sharp rhythm throwing debris in all directions. A near-thrash track with a raw, swirling solo and a killer rhythm section?I stand by it; punchy and explosive. "Enemy In The Garden," the fourth full-length track, features a prog-metal intro that launches Nathan's restrained vocals over guest keyboardist Matt Guillory, James Labrie's regular keyboardist. As you might have guessed, the Dream Theater influence is evident, especially with the solemn break, the pounding pads, and the melting guitar. At one point, you might think you recognize a Pink Floyd vibe, and you wouldn't be wrong. It restarts, highlighting the contrast of this seemingly effortless piece with the excellent second guitar solo. The notes are even higher, and the interplay of vocals and instruments forges the album's standout track. "Ghost Hands," the third acoustic guitar ballad, is simple, effective, gentle, and enchanting. The fragile vocals evoke goosebumps, and the obligatory guitar solo sounds even better; impressively effortless. "Left In The Fire" boasts an intro-riff worthy of Metallica; The cinematic sound brings the power of the machine-gun riff, the keyboard in the background adds the richness to highlight the best notes. It's molten prog metal, resting in its blazing furnace, with Nathan delivering a beautiful vocal performance over a terrifying, savage, tribal rhythmic foundation. A sharp break, the beauty of the acoustic sound before Dean's fiery solo forges a new musical path. The epic arrives, the arpeggio dripping down, delivering the coup de gr�ce to this track. Nick's metronomic drumming guides the finale over the vocal-guitar chord before the delicate outro, a warm acoustic guitar solo, with Nathan's performance moving to the very end.TERAMAZE is back in the saddle after their previous album; here, it's a prog metal masterpiece, blending vocals, rhythm, riffs, edgy melodies, and warm ballads.(4.25)
items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自TERAMAZE的渐进金属专辑，整体风格偏向传统Progressive Metal路线。专辑展现了多样化的音乐元素，从力量金属、重摇滚到原声民谣均有涉及。乐评提及乐队融合了Dream Theater、Kamelot、Fates Warning等主流渐进金属元素，同时穿插了80年代复古摇滚、Punk等风格。"Enemy In The Garden"等曲目体现了Dream Theater式的复杂编曲，"Ghost Hands"则是原声吉他民谣作品。专辑在编曲上具有相当的复杂性，但作为渐进金属作品，其实验性和创新性相对有限，与用户偏好的实验/前卫、电子、爵士等风格存在一定距离，属于Prog Metal领域内较为标准的制作。

items.body: Review by The Progolyte — This very obscure solo artist from Rome by the name of Stefano Testa only has a single album from the seventies under his belt, but I personally think it does more than you think. It's quite pretty, lacking in terms of that overall bombastic sound that I like in most of my Italian music, but still good enough to make an impact. And with an album cover like that, you can tell there's going to be something interesting in here. I think the overall performance could've been more exciting, but the laid-back and relaxed vibes of the material sort of fit well with the more singer-songwriter-oriented music on this record, especially in the second half of the album where the songs get short. Moving on to the personnel, it's Stefano Testa on piano, rhythm guitar, and vocals, and then his band that plays with him consists of Marco Coppi on flute, Alberto Monpellio on moog, Cosimo Fabiano on bass, Ottavio Corbellini on drums, and then Portici takes care of the rest of the guitars. My favorite track on here has to be the grand and thoroughly written sixteen-minute-long suite titled Una Vita. It has various different sections stitched together into one great composition, with mainly more dramatic acoustic bits but also taking use of almost spoken word passages and steady rock rhythms. It's really strong and shows a high level of craftsmanship but is admittedly a little slow and inconsistent in parts. You could say Stefano and the band could've had more enthusiasm in their playing, and though it is strong, it feels lacking when it comes to their overall energy. The rest of the songs are all quite short and uneventful, mainly being simple melodies with limited instrumentation. You can feel like it's going somewhere, but in the end it lies stagnant and doesn't evolve in the way you'd imagine. The highlights from this section were La Ballata Di Achab/Moby Dick and Il Dio Sulla Ferrovia, which had some interesting details such as more progressive structures and sections. In conclusion, this album sort of felt like a letdown, seeing how it had a rating of 4.06 at the time of writing this, but it's still generally an okay record. A bit lacking here and there, not bringing many original ideas to the table, but still a fun one if you like your Rock Progressivo Italiano fit with a lighter and simpler tone. This record will be getting a low 3.5/5.
items._cn_summary: 意大利罗马艺术家 Stefano Testa 于1977年发行的唯一专辑，风格定位为意大利前卫摇滚与歌手创作风格的混合体。专辑整体基调舒缓松弛，第二部分曲目较短，以简单旋律和有限配器为主。最具分量的是时长16分钟的《Una Vita》套曲，展现了戏剧性原声段落与渐进式结构的结合。评论者指出作品虽有创作功底，但整体缺乏能量与热情，部分曲目缺乏发展深度，未能提供足够的原创元素。作为意大利前卫摇滚的独立作品，其文化地域特色可作为加分项，但对于偏好实验性更强、融合度更高的听众而言，该专辑的艺术野心相对有限。

items.body:
Miles Davis, born on May 26, 1926 would turn 100 today. The jazz world is rife with memorials of this centennial and since almost anyone who listens to this music has in some way been touched by Davis' music, we at the Free Jazz Blog thought we would pitch in. It is hardly necessary to introduce the iconic trumpeter - you likely own Kind of Blue and Bitches Brew, right? - and while the musical structures on those albums loosened and spawned entire genres themselves, Davis was somewhat ironically ambivalent in his feelings - if not rather dismissive - towards Free-Jazz overall. Oh well, life is complex. To join in the celebration, Free Jazz Blog collaborator Martin Schray proposed that we do what we like to do the most, write about recordings, chosen from Davis' sprawling discography. We did not set rules - no length, no time periods, overlap of albums was fine, just as long as the pieces reflected the writer's feelings towards the recordings. Today, we start off with Martin's reflections and will continue everyday with new impressions from our critics and a few close associates until there is simply no more to say!- Paul Acquaro 
    Miles Davis- Birth of the Cool (Capitol, 1957) 

    


    In 1949 Capitol signed a contract with the up-and-coming trumpeter Miles
    Davis for a few singles, which he recorded with his nine-piece band that
    same and the following year. The first recordings were initially released on
    78s, then eight tracks appeared for the first time as an album in 1953, on
    10-inch vinyl. Four years later, Capitol released the sessions as an LP with
    eleven tracks. Even at that early stage of his career, one could already see
    what would define Miles Davis throughout his musical life: he was an
    atypical player, yet he possessed remarkable control over timing, dynamics,
    and emotional impact. The pieces gathered here are precise and focused; they
    swing with confidence and move between the immediacy of bebop and the
    sophistication of an Ellington band. Moreover, Davis was a brilliant
    bandleader who was already able to gather the best musicians around him
    (here and even more so later on). Birth of the Cool is
    characterized by the understated elegance of a band that played together
    perfectly, featuring Gerry Mulligan, Kai Winding, John Lewis, Lee Konitz,
    and Max Roach (to name just a few). Gil Evans served as arranger and the
    band’s éminence grise. Ultimately, this album also showcases Davis’s -
    sometimes underestimated- musical prowess. His mostly vibrato-free tone
    could be raw, yet also expressive and vulnerable. Just listen to “Jeru” and
    “Venus de Milo,” true musical masterpieces. Miles Davis- Kind Of Blue (Columbia, 1959) 


    


    In various rankings, John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme and Miles
    Davis’s Kind of Blue are considered the best jazz albums of all
    time. And yet, especially if it comes to Kind of Blue,  connoisseurs of
    harsher, freer music, don’t listen to this albums that often, because it
    allegedly has been played to death - just like “Yesterday” by the Beatles,
    “Smells Like Teen Spirit” by Nirvana, Antonio Vivaldi’s “Four Seasons“, Dave
    Brubeck’s “Take Five”, or Keith Jarrett’s “Köln Concert”. But does that mean
    it has lost its quality over time? Not at all! As to Miles Davis, most hard
    bop players at the time played too much, too long, and too fast. His
    solution: modal playing instead of frantic chord progressions, mid-tempo,
    and plenty of space between the notes. He brought only a few sketches to the
    sessions, yet his choice of ensemble was a compositional masterpiece.  The
    band itself is perhaps the best jazz ensemble that has ever existed:
    Cannonball Adderley’s blues-soaked, relaxed, deep playing meets John
    Coltrane’s daring, modal runs; Bill Evans adds impressionistic touches; Paul
    Chambers’s bass and Jimmy Cobb’s drums are clean, lighthearted, and airy,
    forming a foundation against which the others have complete freedom. Davis’s
    trumpet holds the reins. It’s amazing how this sextet of giants swings. If
    you know “So What“, “Freddie Freeloader“ and “All Blues“ by heart, give
    “Blue in Green“ and “Flamenco Sketches“ a chance and listen closely. You’ll
    feel the magic in every note.  For the second time at the end of a decade,
    Davis shifted the course of music in a different direction. At the end of
    the next decade, he will also determine another change of course.

    Miles Davis- The Complete In A Silent Way Sessions
    (Columbia, 1969) 


    

The next groundbreaking shift in direction, in the late 1960s, was
    
        In A Silent Way. While Columbia’s decision in the late 1990s to release the complete
    sessions for Davis’s most important albums may have been driven by
    commercial interests, for Miles’s fans it’s been  a welcome opportunity to
    witness a work in progress. And nowhere is this more evident than on
    
        In A Silent Way. At the end of the Sixties Miles Davis was playing in half-empty clubs;
    soul, funk, and rock musicians were drawing the kind of audience he would
    have liked to have. For the In A Silent Way sessions between
    September 1968 and February 1969 he therefore wanted an electric bass and an
    electric piano. On The Complete Sessions you can literally feel the
    epochal change in the air. While the first track, “Mademoiselle Mabry,”
    still sounds very much like the old quintet, the change becomes more audible
    with every new musician. In addition to Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock,
    Davis brought in Joe Zawinul as the third keyboardist. The core, now formed
    by three keyboards, and the addition of John McLaughlin as guitarist were
    the quantum leap that ushered in a new era. Davis wanted simple structures
    and hip sounds - nothing complex, and above all, no superfluous chords. The
    result, however, was not jazz-rock, but trippy psychedelic textures that
    also have an ambient quality. But Davis was also concerned with being at the
    cutting edge of the times, both in terms of electronic equipment and
    recording technology. The tried-and-true production techniques no longer
    made sense to him. Teo Macero played a central role as producer, cutting up
    the sessions at specific points and reassembling them. As a musical event
    and group process, what was released back then had never existed before. The
    fact that the record is nonetheless full of the spirit of spontaneous
    improvisation is one of the most astonishing events in recent music history.  A fun fact regarding the reception of this album is that nearly fifteen
    minutes of the LP version consist of exact repetitions, and that this went
    unnoticed and uncommented upon for decades.


    Miles Davis- Bitches Brew (Columbia, 1970) 

Six months after In A Silent Way, Miles Davis ultimately broke with
    the jazz traditionalists. Bitches Brew was even more
    uncompromising, more radical, more challenging. And it was my first Miles
    album. I bought it when I was 18; I needed it for a school presentation.
    When I played it (“Pharaoh’s Dance“, fading in somewhere in the middle and
    then fading out again), most of my classmates were confused. What was that?
    Jazz or rock or something else entirely? I didn’t understand
    
        Bitches Brew
    
    back then (and I’m not sure whether I do it today), but I found the sound
    fascinating. There are few albums I’ve struggled with as much - but it’s
    been worth it. Davis simply took what he started with
    
        In A Silent Way
    
    and cranked it up another two notches. As the recording sessions for
    
        Bitches Brew
    
    approached, he expanded his ensemble once more. Three drum kits, three
    Fender Rhodes, two bassists, and three percussionists - who infused his
    music with African and Indian influences - were tasked with blending jazz
    and rock. He also added Bennie Maupin’s bass clarinet to Wayne Shorter’s sax
    and John McLaughlin’s guitar. The musical motifs he had devised together
    with Wayne Shorter twitched like hummingbirds jolted by electricity. The
    staccato notes from his trumpet ricochet like shrapnels. The collective
    improvisations collapse like flash floods. Additionally, he led the ensemble
    like a conductor who has a rough idea of how the music should sound but had
    to trust his ensemble to make it happen. “If I heard something in the music
    that I thought could be expanded, I gave instructions,” Davis says in his
    biography. The music celebrates the creative process itself; it makes energy
    palpable. Producer Teo Macero hit the record button the moment Davis stepped
    into the studio - whenever an amorphous mass of over a dozen instruments
    coalesced into a collective identity that complemented, repelled, and
    attracted one another. “We didn’t talk much during the recording sessions,”
    Macero said. “After the sessions, I spent weeks in the studio, listening to
    the tapes and beginning to piece the material together.” The result is
    structured free improvisation, which allows plenty of room for individuality
    and often reaches absolute ecstasy, all of which is mercilessly condensed. An album you can listen to forever, one that never bores because it
    completely transcends boundaries. - Martin Schray

items._cn_summary: Free Jazz Blog发表的Miles Davis百年纪念乐评，深入评析了Birth of the Cool与Kind of Blue两张里程碑专辑。评论聚焦于cool jazz的优雅与modal jazz的革新，强调Davis在音色控制、动态把控及乐队领导力上的天赋。Birth of the Cool展现了1949-50年非典型爵士的精致结构，Kind of Blue则被公认为史上最佳爵士专辑之一。然而，这些经典爵士作品虽具有重要历史地位，却与当代实验/前卫/学院派爵士的审美取向存在较大距离。两张专辑均通过主流大厂牌发行，评论内容为原创且质量上乘，但因类型偏向传统爵士且缺乏跨领域融合元素，与用户偏好匹配度有限。

items.excerpt: The Italian luxury fashion house staged a night across two historic venues celebrating Japan’s jazz & kissaten heritage, filmed by Nick Dwyer
items.body:
VIDEO BLOG
A LOOK INSIDE MIU MIU’S INTIMATE TOKYO JAZZ CLUB NIGHT

The Italian luxury fashion house staged a night across two historic venues celebrating Japan’s jazz & kissaten heritage, filmed by Nick Dwyer

WORDS: AMIRA WAWORUNTU | IMAGES: RYOTA CHIBA 27 MAY 2026

On May 13, Italian luxury fashion house Miu Miu held its Jazz Club event in Tokyo, tied to the reopening of its Ginza flagship.

After a cocktail reception at the new store, attendees were invited to two separate venues for the musical programme. The first was Dance Hall Shinseiki, a preserved Showa-era ballroom drawing on Japan’s kissaten listening café tradition and the city's late-night vintage nightlife.

The second was Tokyo Kinema Club, where cabaret and early film culture provided the backdrop for a more immersive experience, culminating in an afterparty.

The event was framed around two Japanese concepts: ma (間), the artistic pause, and shizen (自然), natural emergence, both of which map intuitively onto jazz’s relationship with space and improvisation.


At Dance Hall Shinseiki, the line-up moved through distinct sonic territories.

Tokyo-based multi-instrumentalist Lily opened with a selection deep house, jazz and soul. Hokkaido-born trumpeter, singer-songwriter and producer Reiya Terakubo followed with a live set rooted in jazz but filtered through hip hop, funk and R&B. Grammy-winning pianist and composer Hiromi Uehara closed the ballroom programme with her captivating performance.

The night then moved to Tokyo Kinema Club for the afterparty, headlined by British singer-songwriter Arlo Parks.

The post-event film was directed by Nick Dwyer, the New Zealand filmmaker behind A Century in Sound, who has spent years documenting the city’s music scene.

“Tokyo is often filmed through extremes — neon, chaos, hyper-aestheticism — but the city is infinitely more layered than that,” he tells Mixmag Asia, adding “Anyone who lives here knows there are an infinite number of Tokyos, and the one I inhabit is thankfully a far cry from cliché and hype.”

Read this next: Sound as Medicine: the ancient roots of sonic healing in Asia

That sensibility carries into how he approached Uehara and Terakubo as two artists who occupy different positions within Japanese jazz.

“Reiya is one of the most exciting young jazz artists emerging in Japan right now, and he's searching for his own unique way of contributing to this incredible 70-year history of Japanese jazz. There’s a hunger and curiosity to what he does that feels very exciting to witness,” Dwyer says.


Read this next: The Mixmag Asia Music Guide: Japan

Of Uehara, he adds: “Watching her play live is almost an exercise in transcendence. There’s this extraordinary energy and mastery that completely pulls you in, and I hope viewers can feel even a small part of that experience through this film.”

“In terms of bringing them together cinematically, I think what connects them is a shared devotion to music. They may represent very different moments and expressions within Japanese jazz, but both have dedicated themselves completely to their craft,” he concludes.

Watch the full aftermovie below.

Amira Waworuntu is Mixmag Asia’s Managing Editor, follow her on Instagram.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — HAIZEA (means "wind" in Basque) is one of the more recognized names when it comes to Spain's late70s progressive folk scene from the Basque region and existed from its formation in Hondarribia in1975 until its demise in 1980. The band released two distinct but vastly different albums duringthat time with this self-titled debut more in sync with the Basque folk revival scene that dominatedthe 1960s while the band's second release "Hontz Gaua" explored more daring experimental excursionsinto the world of electric psychedelic folk with much more complex arrangements. While the bandexperienced quite a few lineup changes during its five year run, amazingly the band's two albumsfeatured mostly the same members including vocalist Amaia Zubiria, guitarist / vocalist Xabier Lasa,bassist Gabriel Barrena and drummer Carlos Busto. This debut would be the only album for guitarist /vocalist Txomin Artola who would be replaced with flautist / guitarist Xabier Iriondo on the band'ssecond album.Prog lovers will probably find little interest in this debut as the band was still very much in thetraditional folk revival stage of the previous decade however with all the Basque musical flavorscorrupted by the experimental commingling of progressive rock and psychedelia imported from abroad,this debut does give a crisp clear glimpse into what the world of unaltered Basque folk actuallysounds like and that would be very similar to a lot of other European folk structures despite theBasque language and culture emerging as an anomaly isolate on a continent long overtaken by Indo-European tribes conquering the Paleolithic cultures. Obvious references on this lead to British folkacts such as The Pentangle or Steeleye Span however Basque folk sounds more similar to Celticflavors from not only Spain but the Breton region of France and of course Ireland, Wales and partsof Scotland. No bagpipes here though!While the second album was a crash course in how to update your traditions in the brave new world,HAIZEA's debut is the polar opposite of keeping things as authentic as possible with gentle folkrock instrumentation, a timeless atmospheric presence with all the tracks heavily rooted in the mosttraditional Basque folk melodies sounding much more like a Smithsonian Folkways release ofhistorical recordings than a so-called modern day progressive band but nonetheless the band performsbeautifully with a light airy feel that finds dual male and female vocals trading off along withgentle acoustic arrangements. While the the instrumentation is almost exclusively acoustic, snippetsof electric guitar do seep in on tracks like "Ura Ixurirk." The most notable different betweenBasque folk music and other European flavors is the strange rhythmic patterns that emerge from theband singing exclusively in Euskera, the native term for the Basque language.While this will not be considered essential for those seeking the more adventurous undertakings ofthe second release, this album is beautifully performed and for lovers of ethnic folk musicalexpressions i can't think of a better place to dive into the little known sounds of Basque folklorethan this debut by HAIZEA. The band's name which means "wind" really does shine though on this debutas the album passes by like a nice gentle breeze near the northern coast where Spain and Francemeet. Although there are few traces of anything progressive or experimental on this one it still isworth exploring simply as a point of reference as to how the Basque folk style was incorporated intothe context of prog rock and psychedelic folk from not only the band's sophomore release but themajority of other bands that were jumping on the progressive bandwagon after the collapse of theFranco dictatorship. The final track "Arrosa Xuriaren Azpian" at ten minutes with psychedelicovertones provides a vital clue to the band's next step. As an ethnic music lover i find this onequite pleasant as music like this is like a time machine that gives a glimpse into the collectivesoul of a culture even though i much prefer the good juicy experimental stuff!
items._cn_summary: 西班牙巴斯克地区的传统民谣复兴乐队HAIZEA的1977年首张专辑，以原声乐器为主，融入轻微的迷幻和渐进元素。专辑大量采用巴斯克语演唱，展现了该地区独特的欧斯卡语（Euskera）韵律和节奏模式。双男女声部交替演唱，旋律根植于传统巴斯克民谣，类似英国民谣乐队The Pentangle的风格。虽有少量电吉他点缀，但整体氛围偏向温和的民谣摇滚。对于追求实验性和前卫性的听众而言，此专辑实验性不足，属于较传统的民谣录音；但其巴斯克文化的语言独特性和地区特色提供了一定的人文价值。

items.excerpt: It’s been a lengthy wait for the fourth album from Finnish accordionist Teija Niku , but she’s hardly been idle over the last few years. Between the pandemic, giving birth, and the death of her mother, her time has been filled. But the long pause makes this return all the sweeter, with its joyful exploration of the places where the music of her homeland intersect with her deep love of Balkan music on Tovi .
items.body: Teija Niku - Tovi / a RootsWorld review Teija Niku Tovi Artist release Review by Chris Nickson Tovi by Teija Niku It’s been a lengthy wait for the fourth album from Finnish accordionist Teija Niku, but she’s hardly been idle over the last few years. Between the pandemic, giving birth, and the death of her mother, her time has been filled. But the long pause makes this return all the sweeter, with its joyful exploration of the places where the music of her homeland intersect with her deep love of Balkan music. Tovi by Teija Niku That’s amply illustrated on her composition “Finsko Dajchovo,” inspired by the Bulgarian folk dance rhythm, a loving creation that moves sprightly and gracefully, or “Seitsemän,” taking its cue from Macedonian love songs. The bright, springlike melody, light, full of promise and hope could have been written for eager dancing feet. Everywhere, Niku displays her acute sense of melody. “Elokuu,” a celebration of the late summer lights of August, is a lilting, wistful piece, yet tinged with shades of melancholy for the winter to come, a masterful evocation of shifting moods. Tovi by Teija Niku While the influence of Balkan music hovers over Tovi (the title, according to Niku, translates as “an undefined bit of time, somewhere between a moment and a while”), a Nordic sensibility remains very much at its heart, with a couple of soaring polskas to move things briskly along, in a contrast to the brief, shadowy, brooding opener “Ohto.” Tovi by Teija Niku But the real heart of the disc comes at the very end, with “Poloneesi äidille,” a piece Niku composed for her mother’s 70th birthday, three years before she died. It’s a soft, elegiac work that suddenly becomes transcendent as she begins to sing, You can hear that this performance is completely from the heart, and it is a beautiful way to finish. Now to hope that it’s not such a long gap before she’s back in the studio. Find the artist online. Further listening: Duo Ruut - Ilmateade Maria Moramarco, Fabio Mina, and Francesco Savoretti - Pietrafonie Jaune Toujours - Vertigo
items._cn_summary: 芬兰手风琴演奏家Teija Niku的专辑《Tovi》将芬兰传统音乐与巴尔干民间音乐相融合，以手风琴为主要乐器呈现。专辑收录多首原创曲目，包括受保加利亚舞蹈节奏启发的作品、取材自马其顿情歌的曲目，以及融合波兰舞曲节奏的作品。评论特别提及结尾曲《Poloneesi äidille》，这首为母亲创作的器乐作品在演唱部分展现出真挚的情感表达。作为独立发行作品，专辑展现了芬兰-巴尔干音乐交叉的独特视角，但在实验性和跨界融合方面相对有限，更接近传统世界音乐风格，与用户偏好中的实验/前卫方向存在一定距离。

items.excerpt: Crete’s Stelios Petrakis is at the peak of players of his island’s best-known traditional instrument, the Cretan lyra, a small pear-shaped fiddle held vertically on the knee. True to its title, Lyric is an album of his lyra with a panoply of other traditional instruments played by musicians of equal stature to Petrakis, in music of rich lyricism, in melody and texture.
items.body: Stelios Petrakis - Lyric / a RootsWorld review Stelios Petrakis Lyric Buda Musique Review by Andrew Cronshaw Photo: Claudia de Ventura Crete’s Stelios Petrakis is at the peak of players of his island’s best-known traditional instrument, the Cretan lyra, a small pear-shaped fiddle held vertically on the knee. Its three bowed strings are stopped by the fingernails of the non-bowing hand rather than being pressed to the fingerboard. Its sound hovers on the enticing edge between fundamental and harmonics. Petrakis is also a leading luthier, making the lyras and the other instruments he plays, including the traditional metal-strung lute laouto, and in conjunction with Ross Daly he’s developed and plays a range of lyras with ringing sympathetic strings. True to its title, this an album of his lyra, and laouto, with a panoply of other traditional instruments played by musicians of equal stature to Petrakis, in music of rich lyricism, in melody and texture. “Astro Sti Gaza” (‘Star in Gaza’), a wish for peace written by Petrakis with lyrics by his brother Yannis Petrakis, opens the album. At first a string drone, then Petrakis’s laouto and lyra, Maëlle Duchemin’s harp, Pavlos Spyropoulos’s double bass, and the percussion of Iranian Bijan Chemirani, who plays frame and flask hand-drums on most tracks. The dark, sinuous instrumental line is tracked by the husky vocal of Giorgis Xylouris, who sings on three tracks, the other six being instrumental. “Nathenas,” a traditional Cretan song in asymmetric rhythms, has a powerful ensemble of lyra, laouto, frame-drum, stick-hit davul, topped out by Breton Sylvain Barou’s reeds and Armenian shvi whistle. “Anglianico,” a stately melody composed by Petrakis, has the tremolo mandolins of Valencian musician Efrén López and Michalis Kontaxakis in an elegant almost orchestral sound with lyra, guitars (Antonis Voumvoulakis and Samuel Mele), Spyropoulos’s double bass, and the accordion of Mattia Marco Gregoriadis on whose improvisation the tarantella-like “Pukanè” is based. Chemirani is particularly featured on his composition “Panj Pol,” a short finger-rippling, slapping solo on zarb flask-drum whose rhythm is the foundation for the song that it breaks into, “Agrilos,” by Petrakis with lyrics by brother Yannis celebrating the wine-producing district of Crete where they grew up. It develops into a big sound of massed instruments, with a break on frame-drum and Sakir Oran Uygan’s big double-headed davul drum before a surge of squealing tulum bagpipe and other wind instruments from Barou. “Evlerin Önü Mersin,” a traditional tune from Asia Minor, has a march-like feel, beginning with keening lyra over a slow, inexorable drum pulse, building to soaring epic as more instruments join, peaking with Barou’s zurnas. “Muixeranga,” again with a steady, imposing pulse, is an anthemic tune played in Valencia during the Muixeranga, the traditional building of excitingly high pyramidal human towers in which the big and strong form the bottom layers and the youngest and lightest clamber up to form the topmost. Petrakis intends the track as a message of support to Valencia following the climate-change-driven floods of 2024. Preluded and accompanied by ringing 3/4 time arpeggiating plucked strings and percussion, with the melody played on lyra, the source of “Nothing Else Matters,” is unexpected: it’s a beautiful version, evocative of memory and perhaps sadness, of a Metallica number. Find the artist online. Further listening: Stelios Petrakis Quartet: Spondi Queyras, Sinopoulos, Chemirani: Thrace: Sunday Morning Sessions Ettore Castagna: Eremìa
items._cn_summary: 这张由希腊克里特岛音乐家Stelios Petrakis发行的专辑，以其标志性的克里特里拉琴和劳托为主，融合了伊朗、亚美尼亚、布列塔尼、瓦伦西亚等地区音乐家的演奏，呈现了地中海传统音乐的丰富面貌。评论详细介绍了各曲目的乐器配置与音乐特色，展现了传统器乐在现代语境中的呈现方式。作为独立厂牌Buda Musique发行的世界音乐作品，专辑保持了较高的制作水准和传统音乐的真实感，但在实验性和前卫探索方面相对有限，更倾向于传统民间音乐的自然表达与跨地区融合。

items.album: Don't Drink The Milk - It's Spoiled
items.excerpt: Instrumental funk/soul bands are often spurned by the jazz aficionados as less serious than "real" jazz bands, but that would be a mistake with How Now Brown Cow. Despite the playfulness of the band name and song titles, in addition to having a great deal of fun playing, they are serious musicians and this is seriously good music.
items.body:
Instrumental funk/soul bands are often spurned by the jazz aficionados as less serious than "real" jazz bands, but that would be a mistake with How Now Brown Cow. Despite the playfulness of the band name and song titles, in addition to having a great deal of fun playing, they are serious musicians and this is seriously good music.

How Now Brown Cow has played in the Seattle, Washington community for more than a decade, often as a trio. This live recording from the Sea Monster Lodge, where the band plays regularly, showcases the improvisatory finesse of the band members, from Dave Kurtiak's thick, complicated bass runs to Donovan Pfeifer's solid groove on drums to Kerry O'Connor's funky keyboards. They are supplemented on this recording by Brad Schrandt on sax and flute, a frequent collaborator with the band. His contributions add a forceful texture to the songs and help elevate them even more.

The opener, "No Cat Having Bag," sets the tone for the album. A stomping funky number, the tune is pushed along by Kurtiak's pulsating, busy basslines and Pfeifer's stuttering stickwork, with Schrandt and O'Connor trading solos over the tight rhythm. The members complement each other and engage in keeping the sound fresh and exciting. Even when they slow it down in songs like "Pippity Poppity" and "South of No North," Kurtiak's fingers are moving up and down the bass neck to Pfeifer's steady beat, with O'Connor throwing accents from the keyboards. This is a band on the level of like-minded but better-known bands like Lettuce and Snarky Puppy.

The musical conversations they have on every song are engrossing as well as danceable, especially between O'Connor and Schrandt, working almost as call-and-response at times. The use of flute on a couple of songs offers a different, unexpected flavor. While a more muscular instrument like the sax is expected on funk songs rather than the more delicate flute, Schrandt uses the instrument on "Hang a Louie" to drive the song, while on "That Dog Don't Hunt" he lets the flute float above the cascading keyboard groove O'Connor lays down over a bouncing rhythm from Kurtiak and Pfeiffer.

Based on this recording, the band is definitely one to see live. Although the title is a bit misleading—there is nothing spoiled about this music. Drink it up and you will feel like the psychedelic cow of the cover, well-sated and a little woozy.
items._cn_summary: How Now Brown Cow是一支来自西雅图的器乐funk/soul乐队，这张现场录音展现了乐队十多年的演奏功底，贝斯、鼓和键盘的配合紧密，萨克斯和长笛的加入增添了音色层次。音乐以律动驱动，即兴段落贯穿其中，整体风格偏向传统funk/soul，与Lettuce、Snarky Puppy等知名乐队类似。这种类型化程度较高的器乐放克与用户的实验/前卫、学院派爵士、电子音乐等偏好存在明显距离，音乐中缺乏实验性元素或突破性的声音设计，跨领域融合也不明显。专辑作为扎实的独立funk/soul作品值得关注，但对于追求创新与实验的听众而言吸引力有限。

items.excerpt: A legend has grown up around the music Miles Davis created for Louis Malle's debut film Lift to the Scaffold (Ascenseur pour l'échafaud). The story goes that Davis arrived at the Paris studio having never seen the film. He watched the rushes once, then improvised as the footage rolled with his European quintet—Rene Urtreger on piano, Barney Wilen on tenor saxophone, Pierre Michelot on bass, and Kenny Clarke on drums. The music was recorded on the night of December 4 and 5, 1957.
items.body:
A legend has grown up around the music Miles Davis created for Louis Malle's debut film Lift to the Scaffold (Ascenseur pour l'échafaud). The story goes that Davis arrived at the Paris studio having never seen the film. He watched the rushes once, then improvised as the footage rolled with his European quintet—Rene Urtreger on piano, Barney Wilen on tenor saxophone, Pierre Michelot on bass, and Kenny Clarke on drums. The music was recorded on the night of December 4 and 5, 1957.

The circumstances surrounding the recording are central to its mythology, and the spontaneity was real: Davis was at the peak of his powers.

The film's plot concerns the hired murder of Jeanne Moreau's husband. The professional killer realizes, after the deed is done, that he has left crucial evidence at the scene. Returning to retrieve it, he becomes trapped in the building's lift.

1957 was a landmark year for Davis. In May he had recorded Miles Ahead (Columbia) with Gil Evans. In December came the groundbreaking Lift to the Scaffold sessions—and just four days before those recordings, Davis had played a concert at the Olympia in Paris with the same musicians.

He had come to Paris under contract to appear at the Club Saint-Germain, leaving his regular group behind in New York. By this point he was famous enough to draw crowds on his own. The ensemble he assembled was formidable. Barney Wilen was just twenty, fresh to the scene but already commanding. Pierre Michelot had played with Sidney Bechet and Clifford Brown. René Urtreger was the house pianist at the club and had accompanied Lester Young. Kenny Clarke—who had helped redefine jazz drumming in the 1940s—had made Paris his home. Beyond their residency at Saint-Germain, the group also played concerts in Brussels, Amsterdam, and Stuttgart.

Writer Boris Vian captured the atmosphere of the recording session: "This recording was made at night in the studios of the Paris broadcasting station, in a most informal atmosphere. Among those present was Jeanne Moreau, the principal star of the film. She proved a very charming hostess, serving refreshments to musicians and technicians at an improvised bar. There were those responsible for the production and the technical staff, but also Louis Mall—with his braces dangling loosely—doing his utmost to encourage Miles in his musical accompaniment of the film. The orchestra members, very much at ease in this informal atmosphere, looked at images from the principal scenes and, being thus in the right mood, improvised various musical paraphrases as the reel was projected.

"In the melody 'Dîner au motel' you will notice a curious sonority in Miles' trumpet. The explanation is a strange one: while he was playing, a tiny piece of skin from his lip came loose and stuck in the mouthpiece of his instrument. Miles gladly accepted this strange new element—in the most literal sense, an unheard-of musical effect—in quite the same way as those painters who owe the quality of a particular brushstroke to mere chance."

Little preparation had been done. Davis had sketched only a few simple harmonic sequences in his hotel room and shared them with the band shortly before recording began. With the plot explained, loops of key scenes were projected in the studio while the musicians improvised directly to the images, without any pre-composed themes. Bassist Pierre Michelot later recalled: "Miles just asked us to play two chords—D minor and C7, four bars of each, ad lib." It was typical of Davis: minimal instruction paired with an unerring sense of atmosphere.

By 1957, Davis had grown weary of the dense convolutions of bebop. This challenge gave him permission to slow down—and slow down he does, the music emphasising the film's Hitchcockian tension, its fatal romanticism and nocturnal menace.

Chronologically, the soundtrack sits only months before Kind of Blue (Columbia, 1959), and in many ways it points directly toward that masterpiece. For the first time, Davis fully committed to a modal approach—accepting harmonic limitations not as a constraint but as a means of focusing on pure line, emotion, and tone. As critic Ashley Kahn has noted, "Miles liked the results, and it forever changed how he would approach music and music-making. Eventually, it also changed the jazz world."

Davis's Harmon-muted trumpet is edgy, intimate, and almost corrosive throughout. "Générique" opens the film in an evocative, unhurried mood, giving Davis space to trace the loneliness of Moreau as she wanders the streets. "L'assassinat de Carala" is dark, menacing, and brooding, coiling the film's suspense tighter. "Sur l'autoroute" and "Dîner au motel" drive hard, showcasing Kenny Clarke's crisp brushwork, Wilen's quicksilver tenor, and Michelot's fluent bass. "Florence sur les Champs-Élysées" returns to pacing and melancholic restraint.

The current reissue presents the recordings across three formats. A 180g vinyl LP reproduces the original album in a gatefold tip-on sleeve, with an English translation of Boris Vian's original liner notes. A three-10" vinyl edition expands the release to include the full original soundtrack alongside the complete session takes from December 1957, housed in a three-panel gatefold with Franck Bergerot's essay A Present from Miles Davis to Louis Malle. A limited-edition two-CD set brings together the original album and all surviving takes from the sessions of 4 and 5 December, accompanied by a 60-page hardcover book featuring notes by Ashley Kahn and Franck Bergerot.
items._cn_summary: 1957年Miles Davis为Louis Malle电影《Lift to the Scaffold》即兴创作的爵士配乐专辑，由欧洲五重奏班底在巴黎录音室完成。这张专辑承载着即兴录音的传说与历史意义，属于传统硬咆咆爵士范畴。作品在当时具有一定的电影配乐创新性，但从现代实验/前卫视角审视，其音乐语言相对传统，缺乏显著的实验性元素。专辑虽与用户关注的学院派爵士有交集，却未涉及电子、暗潮或当代古典等跨领域融合。内容来源为allaboutjazz.com，但正文存在截断，完整度不足。考虑到主流厂牌发行及信息不完整的修正，实际评分受限。
