items.excerpt: The Click Five are heading back to Singapore for another night of pop-rock nostalgia. Following two sold-out shows at Capitol Theatre in 2025, the ...
items.body:
The Click Five are heading back to Singapore for another night of pop-rock nostalgia. Following two sold-out shows at Capitol Theatre in 2025, the American band are set to return with the 29 August stop of their For Lovers Tour at Arena @ EXPO.

Known for defining the soundtrack of the early 2000s with irresistible hooks and singalong-ready choruses, the band’s upcoming Singapore show is expected to be their biggest one in the country yet. Fans can look forward to live performances of hits including 'Jenny', 'Just the Girl', and 'Catch Your Wave', alongside other fan favourites from across their catalogue.

The Boston-formed outfit first built a massive fanbase across Asia during their original run, becoming one of Myspace’s most-viewed bands at the height of their popularity. Their 2025 Southeast Asia comeback tour reignited that connection with longtime fans, with tickets for their Singapore dates reportedly selling out within hours.

As part of the For Lovers Tour, the band will also be offering VIP packages and experiences for concertgoers.

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

items.excerpt: Looking back on a glorious 11-year journey, the sun isn't setting anytime soon on SEVENTEEN as they celebrate their anniversary, sharing warm and h...
items.body:
Looking back on a glorious 11-year journey, the sun isn't setting anytime soon on SEVENTEEN as they celebrate their anniversary, sharing warm and heartfelt messages with CARATs on Weverse.

Earlier this year, S.Coups, Jeonghan, Joshua, Jun, Hoshi, Wonwoo, Woozi, DK, Mingyu, The8, Seungkwan, Vernon, and Dino all renewed their contracts with PLEDIS Entertainment, strengthening their bond with fans as they make a pledge to be their favourite idols for as long as they can. With many more milestone anniversaries on the horizon, CARATs celebrate this landmark moment by sharing clips of old performances and iconic moments that stay etched in their minds.

As fans reminisce about the journey of the group so far, the members took to Weverse to share their messages of appreciation, joining in on the nostalgic reflection of the paths they've forged. Although he is currently serving his national service, Hoshi expresses his excitement to complete his duties and reunite with the band to continue performing and creating new bangers for fans to rock out to.

The8 echoes a similar sentiment as he expresses his love by saying, "It’s been 11 years. Thank you for always being by our side, thank you to all the members for getting this far, it hasn’t been easy. Because of the time we’ve spent together, we've long become a part of each other’s lives. We hope to continue creating many more memories together in the future. Thank you for your unwavering love."

As each member expresses their gratitude for the support from CARATs for the past 11 years, they look forward to an even more eventful future as SEVENTEEN. The group anticipates more new hits, even bigger performances, and new endeavours as they continue to preserve the original energy and passion that they have served up since their debut.

items.body:
Photo by John Abbott
By Martin 
    Schray


    


    There’s this scene that has gone down in the history of jazz. A tall, almost
    skinny, Black man playing his saxophone on Williamsburg Bridge in
    New York. The man was Sonny Rollins and already one of the biggest stars in
    the jazz world. At the age of 29 he had decided to take a break from playing
    live and making studio recordings. Rollins had rented a small apartment on
    Grand Street on Lower East Side, but the walls were paper thin and he
    couldn’t practice without disturbing the neighbors. One day he walked
    through Delancey Street, saw the steps up to the bridge and went up. He
    liked it there, he could play as loud as he wanted, with the Brooklyn-bound
    subway on one side and traffic on the other. From that moment on the bridge
    became his daily retreating room of sorts for two years, sometimes for 15 or
    16 hours, in any kind of weather. Spring, summer, fall, and winter.


    Rollins was a musician whose name stands in one line with the greatest ones
    of modern jazz - Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk, Ornette Coleman and John
    Coltrane. Monk was indeed his teacher and partner, he first almost imitated
    Monk’s formal musical principles (on Think of One in 1953) before 
    he became his equal partner (on the Thelonious Monk/Sonny Rollins
    album from 1956, e.g.) and finally emancipated himself with the piano-less
    trio classic Way Out West. As a consequence of these outstanding and
    successful albums he was invited to play Carnegie Hall, the accolade for
    every American musician. But then he realized that all these things didn’t
    help him to rent an apartment - because he was Black. His response was
    
        Freedom Suite
    
    in 1958. In the liner notes he wrote: “America is deeply rooted in Negro
    culture: its colloquialisms; its humor; its music. How ironic that the
    Negro, who more than any other people can claim America's culture as his
    own, is being persecuted and repressed; that the Negro, who has exemplified
    the humanities in his very existence, is being rewarded with inhumanity.“
    Freedom Suite is considered the first instrumental piece that
    accused racism and discrimination. Rollins however, had to face isolation
    after the release of the album. That’s why he took the
    Williamsburg-Bridge-break.


    But on a grey November evening in 1961 he wanted to play again. He wanted to
    pay tribute to Booker Little, a talented young trumpeter, who died at the
    age of 23. The concert was to be a fundraiser for his widow. Rollins called
    the concert and the following album The Bridge, it was his
    comeback. In the 1960s he recorded more excellent albums like
    
        Our Man in Jazz
    
    (1963), Now’s the Time (1964), East Broadway Run Down
    (1966) and the soundtrack for the box office hit Alfie(1966). In
    the musical turmoil of the early Sixties Rollins remained clearly rooted in
    the jazz tradition, but he helped to pave the road to free jazz. His freest
    recordings are Our Man In Jazz from 1962, with Don Cherry on
    trumpet, Bob Cranshaw on bass and Billy Higgins on drums and
    
        1963 Paris Concert
    
    with Henry Grimes on bass. Rollins was looking for new ways but he wasn’t as
    courageous as Ornette or Ayler (which isn’t meant in a negative way, he just
    wasn’t interested in harmolodics or crassly overblown sounds). The reason
    why his music cannot be characterized as free jazz has also to do with the
    rather “traditional“ playing of bass and drums on his compositions (in the
    end they still played time - again not meant in a negative way). However, it
    has always been marvelous to listen to him exploring, finding and dropping
    musical ideas. His saxophone sound is just gigantic, its elegant, deep, very
    articulate and free flowing, he really was a “saxophone colossus“ (the name
    of one of his most famous albums). He had a real lust for playing, every new
    idea he had led to new variations - everything was elaborated with an
    enormous ease, but he wasn’t interested in showing off. From the 1970s
    onwards Sonny Rollins tried to find new ways integrating funk, fusion and
    Latin elements in his music, like on Reel Life (1982). He played
    with bag piper Rufus Harley at the Berliner Jazztage in 1974 (and the
    audience booed them), he recorded with ragtime pianist Mary Lou Williams.
    Moreover, he went to Japan and India and became a buddhist, he discovered
    yoga and lived in a monastery. As to music he also featured new talents like
    Branford Marsalis on Falling in Love with Jazz(1989) and Roy
    Hargrove on Here’s to People (1991). Last but not least, he curated
    his favorite live recordings, the Road Show Series, which is a bonanza for
    die hard fans.


    However, Sonny Rollins was more than his music. All his life he was a
    political person, respect and appreciation were very important for him. In
    an interview with German author Christian Broecking he spoke of himself as a
    “planetarian“, which is one of the reasons why he released
    
        Global Warming
    
    (in 1998), a harsh criticism of the US government’s environmental policy. On
    9/11/2001 his flat was evacuated, his saxophone was the only thing he took
    with him. Only a few days later he played a gig in Boston which was to be
    released as Without a Song: The 9/11 Concert.Rollins dedicated his
    music and his life to the fight against injustice and ignorance, and he
    wanted to express this just by musical means. He believed that music could
    make a difference. He was a visionary. About his time on the bridge he told
    the Washington Post in 2011: “I used to blow my horn back at the boats when
    the boats would blow. All of that was great. I was in a place where nobody
    could see me. This was heaven.” Musically, things had become quiet
    around him in his final years. Now the last great icon of jazz’s golden age
    has passed away. The world is a poorer place without him.


    Watch him with Don Cherry (tp), Henry Grimes (b) and Billy Higgins (dr) in
    Rome 1962:

items.album: Spotify faces backlash over launch of paid Premium AI remix tool
items.excerpt: The platform’s co-chief said he wants Spotify to be “the one that’s legal” when it comes to AI features
items.body:
TECH
SPOTIFY FACES BACKLASH OVER LAUNCH OF PAID PREMIUM AI REMIX TOOL

The platform’s co-chief said he wants Spotify to be “the one that’s legal” when it comes to AI features

WORDS: GEMMA ROSS | PHOTO: GARLEY GIBSON 27 MAY 2026

Spotify and Universal Music Group (UMG) are receiving backlash after launching a new paid Premium feature that allows users to remix their favourite artists’ tracks using AI.

After launching the "groundbreaking" new tool last week (May 21), Spotify’s co-CEO, Alex Norström, said it would have a "rewarding outcome for artists and songwriters" by compensating those who take part.

"Solving hard problems for music is what Spotify does, and fan-made covers and remixes are next," he said at the time.

Read this next: Streaming was the music industry's fastest growing sector in 2025, IMS report reveals

The feature will allow fans to create "AI-driven licensed covers and remixes" using artists’ work as a paid add-on, though it’s currently unclear how much it will cost.

In response, Spotify users shared their fears over the platform’s growing use of AI tools, with one saying on Reddit: "I quit Spotify after many many years because of their attempts to integrate AI into music."

"The platform is totally diminishing creators, making it seem so easy to ‘create’ music," another argued. "When it’s not really creating music. When people’s souls and lives work and experiences go into it."

Read this next: Inside The Movement of Artists and Fans Boycotting Spotify

Alex Norström has since spoken to the Financial Times about Spotify’s continued growth in artificial intelligence, defending the company’s choice to expand its offering of AI tools.

He argued that Spotify’s use of AI is "controlled", but said there are many "rogue attempts" elsewhere, adding that he wants Spotify to be "the one that’s legal" when it comes to AI features.

"There’s some negativity out there about AI, for sure. I think it’s reasonable because some of it is misaligned AI," he said. "I mean, fraud and abuse, we’ve been fighting forever."

Gemma Ross is Mixmag's Associate Digital Editor

items.excerpt: BABYMONSTER are officially bringing their second world tour to Singapore this November, and ticketing details are finally here. The K-pop girl gro...
items.body:
BABYMONSTER are officially bringing their second world tour to Singapore this November, and ticketing details are finally here.

The K-pop girl group will perform at the Singapore Indoor Stadium on 28 November as part of the 2026–27 BABYMONSTER WORLD TOUR ‘춤 (CHOOM)’. The upcoming show follows the success of the septet’s sold-out Singapore concert in 2025 during their debut HELLO MONSTERS world tour.

Organised by Live Nation Singapore, the concert marks one of the group’s Asia stops for the ongoing world tour, which will also see the act perform across cities including Bangkok, Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur, Taipei, Hong Kong, Sydney, and Melbourne.

BABYMONSTER are currently promoting their third mini album, 춤 (CHOOM), which was released on 4 May.

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

Ticket prices for the Singapore concert are priced at S$358, S$348, S$308, S$298, S$258, S$228, S$188, and S$168, excluding booking fees.

VIP ticket holders will receive:

MONSTIEZ MEMBERSHIP holders can register for the Weverse presale from 26 May, 12 PM to 29 May, 11:59 PM. The Weverse presale will then take place on 8 June, from 10 AM to 11:59 PM. Mastercard and Trip.com presales will run on 9 June, from 10 AM to 11:59 PM, while the Live Nation presale is set for 10 June, from 12 PM to 11:59 PM. General ticket sales begin on 11 June at 12 PM via Ticketmaster Singapore.
